texto:
We are raising the policy rate to dampen inflation

Introductory statement by Governor Ida Wolden Bache at the press conference following the announcement of the policy rate on 24 September 2026.

Download presentation (pdf)

Chart: Policy rate raised to 4.5 percent

The Monetary Policy and Financial Stability Committee has decided to raise the policy rate by 0.25 percentage point to 4.5 percent.

Norges Bank is tasked with keeping inflation close to 2 percent over time. We are also mandated to help keep employment as high as possible and to promote economic stability.

Chart: Inflation has been above target for several years

Inflation has been above target for several years. By raising the policy rate, we are helping to reduce inflation. It will likely be necessary to keep the policy rate elevated for a time, and the Committee is prepared to raise the policy rate further if needed to bring inflation down to target within a reasonable time horizon.

Let me say a bit more about the background for the decision and the Committee’s assessments.

Figures released earlier this month show consumer price inflation of 3.3 percent. Adjusted for tax changes and excluding energy products, inflation was 3.0 percent.

High inflation over time can make inflation stickier and harder to bring down again. In June, when we last presented projections, the Committee judged that it would likely be necessary to raise the policy rate at one of the forthcoming meetings. Over the summer, underlying inflation moderated and was lower than expected. But the inflation outlook somewhat further ahead does not appear to have changed materially.

Chart: Oil and gas prices have risen

The sharp rise in firms’ labour costs in recent years will contribute to keeping inflation elevated ahead. At the same time, the conflict in the Middle East is still creating uncertainty about the inflation outlook, and since June, prices for oil and gas and various other commodities have risen. Higher energy and commodity prices will result in higher costs for many domestic firms and higher prices for imported consumer goods. On the other hand, the krone has appreciated so far this year and is now stronger than assumed in the June projections. A stronger krone will in isolation pull down inflation.

Chart: Monetary policy tightening expected abroad

Higher energy and commodity prices are also pushing up inflation internationally, and market rates have increased considerably since June. In recent weeks, US and euro area policy rates were raised, and more rate hikes are expected in the US, the euro area and various other countries. Long-term interest rates have also increased. Higher interest rates abroad pull in the direction of higher interest rates also in Norway, among other things, through the effect on the krone exchange rate.

Chart: Firms report that it has become easier to recruit labour

When we set the policy rate, we also give weight to employment. We do not want to restrict the economy more than needed. In recent years, the Norwegian economy has gradually cooled and our Regional Network contacts report that it has become easier to recruit labour. Nevertheless, unemployment has shown little change over the past year. In August, 2.1 percent of the labour force was registered as fully unemployed, in line with our projection.

Chart: An elevated policy rate likely necessary for a time

In the policy rate forecast presented today, the policy rate remains close to the current level for a period ahead before declining somewhat. The forecast indicates that the policy rate will remain elevated somewhat longer than indicated by the June forecast.

Chart: Inflation down to target without a marked increase in unemployment

Inflation is projected to slow from next year and move down to 2 percent in 2029. The economy is expected to cool somewhat further, and registered unemployment is projected to edge up to slightly above pre-pandemic levels.

Wage growth is expected to be lower this year than in 2025 and to slow further in the years ahead. With lower inflation, household purchasing power is still expected to continue to strengthen, also when factoring in interest expenses.

The economic outlook is uncertain and hence also interest rate developments. In any case, we will set the policy rate with the aim of returning inflation to target.

More information

Policy rate decision September 2026

titulo: Schweigaard lecture: Ten questions and answers about monetary policy
contexto_listado: Schweigaard lecture: Ten questions and answers about monetary policy
texto:
Schweigaard lecture: Ten questions and answers about monetary policy

Good morning, everyone. I would like to thank the Department of Economics at the University of Oslo for inviting me to give this year’s Schweigaard Lecture.

Choosing a theme was not difficult. Since inflation surged in spring 2022, and Norges Bank responded by raising the policy rate substantially and rapidly, monetary policy has been a subject of debate in Norway.

One view, put forward by the Norwegian Confederation of Trade Unions (LO), is that Norges Bank has placed too much weight on inflation and too little on employment when setting the policy rate. From parts of academia, on the other hand, we have been criticised for taking too long to tackle inflation. Former Deputy Director of the Norwegian Directorate of Health, Espen Rostrup Nakstad, has questioned whether the policy rate is even suited to bringing down inflation.

Monetary policy is also being debated internationally. In several countries, central banks’ monetary policy independence has been challenged in recent years, and in the US the new Federal Reserve Chair has rekindled the debate on how much central banks should, or should not, say about monetary policy.

It is not surprising that monetary policy generates debate. Interest rates matter greatly to people’s finances, not least here in Norway. Debate has its place in a democracy. The announcement last year that the Ministry of Finance would review the monetary policy mandate does not make the debate less relevant.

And let me stress that I am not saying that economists should be the only group participating in the debate about monetary policy. Doctors are also welcome.

I will use today’s lecture to answer some of the questions that have been raised. So let me begin:

1. Why is inflation at 2 percent so important?

This question goes to the very core of Norges Bank’s mission. It is now 25 years since inflation targeting was introduced in Norway. Since 2018, the target has been 2 percent.

Chart: “Inflation”

Most people would agree that low and stable inflation is a good thing. When prices suddenly rose sharply four or five years ago, the costs of high inflation were widely felt.

When prices rise quickly and unexpectedly, it becomes hard to plan and make good decisions. High inflation makes it difficult, for example, to know whether the price of a good or service is reasonable, and wage increases that look generous when they are agreed may after a few months be eroded by high inflation. The lowest income groups are most affected by rapid and unexpected price increases.

Low and stable inflation is a precondition for a well-functioning economy. At the same time, some inflation is good. It makes the economy more flexible and keeps deflation, a sustained fall in prices, at a distance. Historically, deflation is associated with economic stagnation and high unemployment.

It is therefore wise to aim for an inflation rate that is neither too high nor too low. In Norway, as in a number of other countries, we settled on an inflation target of 2 percent. This provides a reasonable balance between the two aims.

This does not mean that the economy would necessarily have performed substantially worse if we had chosen a slightly higher target. But those who might imagine that a higher inflation target would provide room for a permanently lower interest rate would be disappointed. Over time, what matters for how interest rates affect the economy is the real interest rate, that is, the interest rate less inflation. Had we chosen a higher inflation target, the policy rate would also have been higher on average.

2. Does Norges Bank give too little weight to the aim of keeping employment as high as possible?

In the debate this is what some people have opined, arguing that the policy rate increases in recent years have pushed up unemployment too much. So let me say a little more about the trade-offs we make when setting the policy rate.

Sustaining employment at the highest possible level is an overriding objective of economic policy, which Norges Bank is also mandated to promote. The mandate assigned to us by the political authorities provides for a flexible inflation targeting regime, so that monetary policy can also contribute to high employment and economic stability.

Over time, there is no conflict between the objectives of low and stable inflation and high employment. In the long run, we cannot trade off higher employment for higher inflation. Quite the contrary. Low and stable inflation is important for a well-functioning economy and provides the best possible basis for keeping employment as high as possible.

In the short term, however, a conflict may arise between the two aims. A higher policy rate will dampen inflation but also restrain economic activity, which may lead to higher unemployment.

When setting the policy rate, we seek to strike the right balance between these aims.

Chart: “Unemployment and inflation”

In recent years, the policy rate has helped cool the economy. Unemployment has edged up from a low level. Inflation has come down substantially from the peak but is still above target. With a higher policy rate, we could have brought inflation down faster. But we do not want to restrict the economy more than needed. We are therefore taking time to bring inflation back to target.

However, there is a limit to how much time we can take. Over time, high inflation can lead households and firms to begin planning for greater inflation persistence. For example, firms set their selling prices for a period ahead based on expected price and cost changes. If inflation has been high for a long time, firms may assume that it will remain so and raise their own selling prices. Such mechanisms entail a risk of greater inflation persistence, making it more difficult to bring inflation down again. In situations like the present, when inflation has remained above target for a long time, we are therefore particularly alert to signs of rising inflation pressures.

Financial market participants generally assume that we will react to an elevated inflation outlook by tightening monetary policy. That confidence in the inflation target is valuable and helps us keep inflation low and stable. If we over time do not react to an elevated inflation outlook, we could risk eroding confidence in the inflation target. The krone could then weaken markedly, and prices continue to rise rapidly. Should that happen, a sharp increase in the policy rate would be needed to bring inflation down again, with potentially high costs in the form of job losses.

3. Should the green transition become a monetary policy objective?

So, when setting the policy rate we must give weight to keeping employment as high as possible. Economic policy must also take other important considerations into account such as equitable distribution and sustainable development. It has been argued that Norges Bank should use the policy rate to promote more objectives than those set out in the current mandate. A concrete question that has been raised is whether Norges Bank should use the policy rate to promote the green transition.

In my view, the answer to this question should be no. We also expressed this view in our submission on the review of the monetary policy mandate earlier this year.

And this is not because I consider the objective to be unimportant. One of the greatest challenges of our time is to succeed in the transition to a low-carbon economy. The objective of low and stable inflation may perhaps seem trivial in that context.

The economy is increasingly affected by climate change and measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. This summer, we have once again seen how heatwaves, droughts and fires in Europe cause extensive damage. Such events can have consequences for inflation, output and employment, which we must take into account when setting the policy rate. However, I would caution against using monetary policy to address climate challenges.

First and foremost, this is because monetary policy is ill-suited to the task. The policy rate is not an effective instrument for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Other components of economic policy have far more targeted instruments, such as carbon taxes, emissions trading systems and regulation.

In our view, monetary policy’s most important contribution to the climate transition is to ensure low and stable inflation over time. Low and stable inflation provides a safer environment for making needed climate-related investments. When inflation is low, it is also easier to distinguish changes in individual prices from general inflation, strengthening the signal from, for example, higher carbon taxes.

4. Why is a handful of economists allowed to decide the price of borrowing money?

Interest rates have a substantial impact on the finances of both households and firms. Nevertheless, politicians have entrusted policy rate setting to five economists.

The five Committee members are me, the two Deputy Governors, Pål Longva and Øystein Børsum, and the two external members, Steinar Holden and Hilde C. Bjørnland, both professors of economics. Together, we constitute the Monetary Policy and Financial Stability Committee.

If we go far back in time, the monetary system was controlled by the king. During the Napoleonic Wars, the system failed. To finance the war, the king printed ever more money. Inflation spiralled out of control, and people lost confidence in money.

This does not mean that elected representatives have abdicated. Even though the Committee sets the policy rate, politicians decide our aims and objectives.

The debate in Norway shows that politicians are attentive to interest rate developments. Nevertheless, during my time as Governor, I have not experienced Norwegian politicians challenging the central bank’s monetary policy independence, as has occurred in other countries.

Let me emphasise that when we at Norges Bank highlight the importance of central bank independence, it is not for our own sake, but because delegating the conduct of monetary policy to an independent central bank has proved to be the most effective way of ensuring price stability. International experience also indicates that if doubts arise about central bank independence, investors may adjust their inflation expectations and demand higher risk premiums.

5. Does Norges Bank believe that higher interest rates can bring down prices abroad?

The answer is no, and I doubt there are many people who actually believe that we believe so. But some have argued that we should not raise the policy rate when part of the reason for high inflation is that prices for oil and other international commodities have risen as a result of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East.

We cannot, of course, influence prices abroad, but that does not mean we should disregard them when setting the policy rate.

Although we cannot influence prices abroad, we can influence spillovers to domestic prices and counteract the onset of a rise in prices for a broad range of goods and services due to higher commodity prices. A stronger krone will also reduce export profitability and may thereby help dampen wage growth.

We will normally respond less forcefully with the policy rate when inflation is caused by an imported cost shock that also dampens economic activity than when inflation is driven by high demand and strong pressures in the economy.

Everything I have said so far rests on a fundamental premise: that a higher policy rate actually helps bring inflation down.

But can a high policy rate be the wrong medicine for bringing inflation down? May it even be that a lower policy rate would have resulted in lower inflation? These questions were raised in the debate earlier this year.

We see that inflation is often high when the policy rate is high, but this does not mean that a higher policy rate leads to higher inflation. It could just as well be the case that the central bank raises the policy rate precisely because inflation is high.

The fact that high inflation leads to a high policy rate makes measuring the impact of rate changes challenging but not impossible. Our methods allow us to distinguish the policy rate’s response to inflation from the effect of the policy rate on inflation. When such methods are applied, the results are quite clear. This does not mean, however, that no prices rise when interest rates rise. Rents are a case in point. When interest rates rise, landlords’ costs increase and they may attempt to pass these costs on to tenants through higher rents. This mechanism is supported by research and is an example of what economists call the cost channel.

Yet, it is still the case that a higher policy rate dampens overall inflation. The reason is that there are other, stronger, channels from higher interest rates to inflation. Households tighten consumption and firms postpone investment in response to higher interest rates. This dampens economic activity, which in turn leads to lower wage and price inflation over time. A higher policy rate also strengthens the krone, which reduces prices for imported goods.

So, the answer to the question is yes, the policy rate is the right medicine for bringing inflation down. Our job at Norges Bank is to find the right dosage.

In both Sweden and Denmark, interest rates have come down substantially from their peak in 2024. The policy rate in Norway is now more than 2 percentage points higher than in our closest neighbouring countries. This makes many people wonder why we could not have simply lowered our policy rate too.

There are many similarities across the Scandinavian countries, but in order to answer this question I will begin with an important distinction. While Norway and Sweden have a floating exchange rate, Denmark has chosen to peg its currency to the euro. The forecast is not a promise but shows what we consider to be the most likely policy rate path given our mandate and our assessment of economic developments.

Transparency about the basis for our decisions is important for democratic oversight and for enabling the public to hold us to account. We also seek to be transparent about how monetary policy will react to changes in the economic outlook. But this approach also implies some dilemmas. Greater transparency is not necessarily synonymous with better communication. One argument against publishing a policy rate forecast is that it may be perceived as a promise, and that frequent revisions to the rate path can weaken confidence in the central bank.

The best suited approach to communication can vary across countries and change over time. We are following the international debate with great interest. In any event, we will continue to be transparent, continue to answer questions and continue to explain our rate decisions. I won’t become taciturn.

9. What are the implications of AI for monetary policy?

The world is undergoing an epochal shift in technology. Some people have asked me what the implications of AI will be for the monetary policy stance. The answer is that I do not know, and perhaps this is not the most important question to ask about the consequences of AI. But how new technology affects the economy is naturally a matter of interest to both Norges Bank and other central banks. Others believe productivity may initially fall because new technology requires time, investment and adjustment before the gains are realised.

10. Where is the policy rate headed?

The final question I will answer today is also the question I am asked most often, which is how the policy rate will evolve ahead. The short answer is that it depends on economic developments. I also have a longer answer, which is based on the forecasts we presented in June and the assessments we made at our monetary policy meeting earlier this month.

Unemployment in Norway is now neither especially high nor unusually low. Inflation, however, is too high and has run above target for several years.

An important reason why inflation remains elevated is that firms’ labour costs have risen substantially in recent years. Wage growth has not been high relative to profitability in manufacturing. The principle of the Norwegian wage determination model is precisely that workers should receive their share of value added in manufacturing. But wage growth raises firms’ costs, and although wage growth is slowing, it will continue to keep inflation elevated.

It is our assessment that a restrictive monetary policy stance is needed to return inflation to target within a reasonable time horizon. Our June policy rate forecast indicated an increase in the policy rate from 4.25 percent to just above 4.5 percent by the end of the year. We envisaged raising the policy rate at one of the forthcoming monetary policy meetings.

Chart: “Policy rate forecasts since 2021”

But as this chart clearly shows, the policy rate forecast is neither a promise nor a definitive roadmap. As I already touched on, in recent years we have had to revise our policy rate forecasts substantially because the economic outlook has changed.

Inflation fell this summer and has been lower than projected. Slower inflation is welcome news, but inflation is still markedly above target, and it is too early to conclude that the inflation outlook has changed materially. It may thus still become necessary to raise the policy rate.

In about a month, we will present new forecasts. Experience suggests that they are unlikely to be identical to those we presented in June. What remains unchanged is that we will set the policy rate with the aim of returning inflation to target within a reasonable time horizon.

Many wonder when the policy rate will come down. If we look somewhat further ahead and with inflation moving towards target, it will probably be appropriate to begin a prudent easing of monetary policy. However, as the chart shows, we do not envisage that the policy rate will be significantly lower ahead. For borrowers, that may be one of the most important takeaways from this lecture.

Thank you for your attention. And to those of you who are just beginning your studies, I wish you the best of luck. There has rarely been a more interesting time to be a student. My advice is to use this unique time to learn, not only from your lecturers, but from one another. Be curious and dare to ask the big questions.

The announcement last year that the Ministry of Finance would review the monetary policy mandate does not make the debate less relevant.

This question goes to the very core of Norges Bank’s mission. It is now 25 years since inflation targeting was introduced in Norway. Since 2018, the target has been 2 percent.

The lowest income groups are most affected by rapid and unexpected price increases.

Low and stable inflation is a precondition for a well-functioning economy. At the same time, some inflation is good. It makes the economy more flexible and keeps deflation, a sustained fall in prices, at a distance. Historically, deflation is associated with economic stagnation and high unemployment.

The best suited approach to communication can vary across countries and change over time. We are following the international debate with great interest. We have no specific plans to implement any changes at present, but we are continuously working to enhance our communication of monetary policy and our response pattern.
In any event, we will continue to be transparent, continue to answer questions and continue to explain our rate decisions. I won’t become taciturn.
9. What are the implications of AI for monetary policy?

The world is undergoing an epochal shift in technology. Some people have asked me what the implications of AI will be for the monetary policy stance. The answer is that I do not know, and perhaps this is not the most important question to ask about the consequences of AI. But how new technology affects the economy is naturally a matter of interest to both Norges Bank and other central banks. AI can clearly perform many tasks faster and better and spur new ideas and solutions. However, the magnitude of productivity gains and how quickly they will materialise are uncertain. Researchers’ estimates vary widely. Some expect substantial gains. Others believe productivity may initially fall because new technology requires time, investment and adjustment before the gains are realised.
But if we assume that productivity will increase, will this result in higher or lower interest rates? The answer partly depends on the time horizon.

If AI boosts global productivity, growth opportunities will increase and the willingness to invest could pick up. The interest rate level could then become higher over time than it would otherwise have been, both globally and in Norway.

In the near term, higher productivity could reduce firms’ production costs and dampen inflation, which pulls in the direction of lower policy rates. However, if expectations of higher earnings and wage growth were to boost investment and consumption without the supply side keeping pace, both wage and price inflation could pick up. Policy rates could then rise – also in the near term.

AI may have far-reaching consequences for the economy and for Norges Bank’s tasks. It is precisely in the face of ever-changing economic conditions that it is sensible to conduct regular reviews of the mandate for monetary policy, as announced by the Ministry of Finance.

I believe that we currently have a sound mandate. In my view, flexible inflation targeting has functioned well, and I cannot foresee a better alternative at the present time. Whether it will also be the best alternative in the future remains to be seen.
10. Where is the policy rate headed?

The final question I will answer today is also the question I am asked most often, which is how the policy rate will evolve ahead. The short answer is that it depends on economic developments. I also have a longer answer, which is based on the forecasts we presented in June and the assessments we made at our monetary policy meeting earlier this month.
Unemployment in Norway is now neither especially high nor unusually low. Inflation, however, is too high and has run above target for several years.

An important reason why inflation remains elevated is that firms’ labour costs have risen substantially in recent years. Wage growth has not been high relative to profitability in manufacturing. The principle of the Norwegian wage determination model is precisely that workers should receive their share of value added in manufacturing. But wage growth raises firms’ costs, and although wage growth is slowing, it will continue to keep inflation elevated.

It is our assessment that a restrictive monetary policy stance is needed to return inflation to target within a reasonable time horizon. Our June policy rate forecast indicated an increase in the policy rate from 4.25 percent to just above 4.5 percent by the end of the year. We envisaged raising the policy rate at one of the forthcoming monetary policy meetings.
Chart: “Policy rate forecasts since 2021”

But as this chart clearly shows, the policy rate forecast is neither a promise nor a definitive roadmap. As I already touched on, in recent years we have had to revise our policy rate forecasts substantially because the economic outlook has changed.

Inflation fell this summer and has been lower than projected. Slower inflation is welcome news, but inflation is still markedly above target, and it is too early to conclude that the inflation outlook has changed materially. It may thus still become necessary to raise the policy rate.

In about a month, we will present new forecasts. Experience suggests that they are unlikely to be identical to those we presented in June. What remains unchanged is that we will set the policy rate with the aim of returning inflation to target within a reasonable time horizon.

Many wonder when the policy rate will come down. If we look somewhat further ahead and with inflation moving towards target, it will probably be appropriate to begin a prudent easing of monetary policy. However, as the chart shows, we do not envisage that the policy rate will be significantly lower ahead. For borrowers, that may be one of the most important takeaways from this lecture.

Thank you for your attention. And to those of you who are just beginning your studies, I wish you the best of luck. There has rarely been a more interesting time to be a student. My advice is to use this unique time to learn, not only from your lecturers, but from one another. Be curious and dare to ask the big questions.

Monetary Policy Statement, 2026-27 Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee October 5 to 7, 2026

Monetary Policy Decisions The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) held its 63rd meeting from October 5 to 7, 2026, under the chairmanship of Shri Sanjay Malhotra, Governor, Reserve Bank of India. The MPC members Dr. Nagesh Kumar, Shri Saugata Bhattacharya, Prof. Ram Singh, Dr. Poonam Gupta and Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya attended the meeting. 2. After a detailed assessment of the evolving macroeconomic and financial developments and the outlook, the MPC voted unanimously to increase the policy repo rate under the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) by 25 bps to 5.50 per cent. Consequently, the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate stands adjusted at 5.25 per cent and the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate and the Bank Rate at 5.75 per cent. The MPC also decided to change the stance to calibrated tightening. Growth and Inflation Outlook Global Outlook 3. Since the last MPC meeting in August 2026, the re-escalation of the conflict in West Asia and the consequent sharp volatility in crude oil prices has kept the global economy in a state of flux. Global growth has remained resilient. Acceleration of inflation in key economies has prompted a shift towards hawkish monetary policy. The US Fed hiked by 25 bps in September. The Fed commentary thereafter along with rate tightening by major systemically important central banks have reinforced expectations of higher global policy rates. Tighter global financial market conditions coupled with fiscal sustainability concerns in major economies are keeping global bond yields at record high levels. With a resolution of the West Asia conflict remaining elusive, significant downside risks to the global outlook remain, including further tightening of global financial conditions, continuing elevated AI-related asset valuations and high public debt. Domestic Outlook 4. Notwithstanding these persisting global headwinds, the Indian economy has remained resilient. As per National Statistics Office (NSO) estimates, real GDP growth in Q1:2026-27 at 7.8 per cent was higher than expected. Strong private consumption and fixed investment, rebound in merchandise exports and sustained buoyancy in services exports supported growth. On the supply side, the manufacturing sector grew at a robust pace. Services sector activity strengthened further, owing to buoyant domestic and external demand. 5. In Q2, available high frequency indicators for July-August suggest sustained momentum in domestic economic activity. Domestic demand remains resilient and is well supported by robust external demand with merchandise exports registering double-digit growth. 6. Looking ahead, global economic uncertainty will continue to have some bearing on domestic economic activity. While energy prices and supply chain pressures have continued, their near-term trajectory remains uncertain amidst the lingering West Asia conflict. Their adverse impact is being contained with active diversification of supply sources. Deficient south-west monsoon and strong El Niño conditions pose risks to agriculture sector’s outlook and rural demand, although healthy buffer of foodgrains and proactive policy interventions by the government are expected to mitigate the impact. Furthermore, continuing momentum in services and broadly stable employment conditions are likely to support urban demand. Strong capacity utilisation, robust credit flows and the government’s thrust on infrastructure are expected to sustain investment activity. While services exports are expected to remain buoyant, bilateral trade agreements should boost merchandise exports. 7. Taking all these factors into consideration, real GDP growth for 2026-27 is projected at 7.1 per cent, with Q2 at 7.2 per cent; Q3 at 6.9 per cent and Q4 at 6.8 per cent. Real GDP growth for Q1:2027-28 is projected at 7.1 per cent. The risks are evenly balanced ( Chart 1 ). 8. CPI inflation increased to 4.8 per cent in August 2026 from 4.5 per cent in July. While the increase has been predominantly on account of higher inflation in food and fuel groups, core inflation has also picked up indicating some signs of widening price pressures. Food price increases have become more broad based along with notable spikes in certain items such as sugar and onion. The uptick in fuel inflation in August largely reflected unfavourable base effects. Core inflation increased to 4.2 per cent and core inflation, excluding precious metals, increased to 2.9 per cent in August. The weighted share of items in headline CPI recording inflation above 4 per cent increased steadily to about 37 per cent in August. 9. The near-term outlook on inflation points towards continued pressures from supply side on account of the deficient monsoon, ongoing El Niño conditions and high energy and other commodity prices, the pass through of which is still continuing. Considering all factors, CPI inflation is projected to be 5.2 per cent for 2026-27 with Q2 at 4.9 per cent; Q3 at 6.0 per cent; and Q4 at 5.7 per cent ( Chart 2 ). Inflation for Q1:2027-28 is projected at 5.6 per cent with risks being evenly balanced. Core inflation is projected at 4.4 per cent for 2026-27. Rationale for Monetary Policy Decisions 10. The MPC noted that the global context on account of geopolitical developments remains challenging. Nonetheless, the Indian economy has been strong. The economic momentum remains broad-based. The economy is expected to remain resilient. 11. In the light of available data, it is clear that inflation and its outlook are not benign as they were last year with headline CPI inflation expected to average almost 5.8 per cent in the next three quarters and core inflation projected at 4.4 per cent this year. In this milieu, recalibrating the policy rate is imperative. 12. As regards supply side inflation, monetary policy primarily acts by curtailing second round effects (inflation expectations and firm level pricing behaviour, etc.), which take time to manifest and are difficult to extract from available data. Apart from data related to inflation expectations and firm level pricing behaviour, indicators of generalisation of inflation like core inflation and diffusion indices are used for this purpose. It may, however, be kept in mind that it is difficult to distinguish between the second-round effects and the indirect impact of supply side pressures (in production cost through energy and other inputs) as both are present in these indicators. While there is some evidence of elevated inflation expectations and generalisation of inflation, there are only limited signs of supply side pressures getting embedded in pricing behaviour. 13. Similarly, while there is limited evidence of demand side pressures, risks in view of strong growth in monetary and credit aggregates exist. 14. Considering all these factors, the MPC unanimously voted to increase the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent. The MPC also decided to change the stance to calibrated tightening. It only signals that given the current conditions, rate cuts are off the table in the near term and policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause, depending on the evolving conditions and the outlook. The duration and extent of rate hike cycle would be contingent on the actual growth-inflation developments and outlook, especially that of underlying inflation, the extent of broadening of price pressures and second round effects of the supply shock, as also the impact of demand impulses. 15. Two members - Dr. Nagesh Kumar and Prof. Ram Singh - were of the view that the stance be retained at neutral. 16. The MPC remains committed to its price stability mandate and will endeavour to progressively align inflation with its target. 17. The minutes of the MPC’s meeting will be published on October 21, 2026. 18. The next meeting of the MPC is scheduled for December 2 to 4, 2026. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1264

Monetary Policy Report – October 2026

Contents Chapter I: External Environment I.1: Global Economic Conditions I.2: Commodity Prices and Inflation I.3: Monetary Policy Stance I.4: Financial Markets I.5: Conclusion Box I.1: The Stock–Bond Correlation in Advanced and Emerging Economies Chapter II: Liquidity Conditions and Financial Markets II.1: Liquidity Conditions and the Operating Procedure of Monetary Policy II.2: Domestic Financial Markets II.3: Transmission to Lending and Deposit Rates II.4: Conclusion Box: II.1: Drivers of CD and CP Rate Spreads Box: II.2: Bank Lending Channel of Monetary Policy: A Sectoral Approach Chapter III: Demand and Output III.1: Aggregate Demand III.2: Aggregate Supply III.3: Conclusion Box III.1: Indian Agricultural Sector amidst Weather Shocks Chapter IV: Prices and Costs IV.1: Introduction IV.2: Developments across Major Components of the CPI IV.3: Decoding the Inflation Dynamics IV.4: Drivers of Inflation Trajectory IV.5: Conclusion Box IV.1: Measuring Inflation Generalisation through the Diffusion Index Box IV.2: What Drives Inflation in India? Disentangling Demand and Supply Factors Chapter V: Macroeconomic Outlook V.1: Key Developments since the April 2026 MPR V.2: Inflation Outlook V.3: Growth Outlook V.4: Balance of Risks V.5: Conclusion Box V.1: Crude Oil Price Shocks: Quantifying the Macroeconomic Impact on the Indian Economy Abbreviations Executive Summary Global growth remained resilient in 2026 so far, supported by AI-related investment, and fiscal stimulus measures, despite disruptions due to the ongoing West Asia conflict. Renewed energy-price pressures stoked inflation pressures and prompted a more hawkish stance from leading central bank. Fiscal sustainability concerns, persistent inflation, and geopolitical uncertainty raised bond yields, while equity markets remained volatile amid lingering concern on valuations technology stocks. Amidst global uncertainty, domestic financial markets underwent intermittent volatility during H1:2026-27. System liquidity surplus surged in September 2026, mainly on account of the Reserve Bank’s swap facilities. Overnight rates in the money market evolved in sync with prevailing liquidity conditions. Transmission to lending and deposit rates plateaued with status quo in policy rate during H1:2026-27. Bank credit growth became broad based and strengthened further. The domestic economy showed resilience in H1:2026-27, despite continued global uncertainty amidst the conflict. The supply-side pressures were alleviated by proactive policy measures by the government that ensured adequate supply of key inputs. Real GDP recorded a growth of 7.8 per cent in Q1:2026-27 reflecting strong momentum in underlying economic activity. Aggregate demand remained strong on the back of both private consumption and investment. Net external demand was also robust and contributed significantly to growth. On the supply side, both manufacturing and services sectors recorded strong growth in Q1. High frequency indicators suggest continued buoyancy in domestic economic activity, albeit with some moderation compared to Q1. Stable employment conditions, congenial financial conditions, revival in corporate investment, and a pickup in goods exports – nurtured by bilateral FTAs and diversification – are expected to support economic activity going forward. Sustenance of private consumption growth will be essential for broad-based recovery in private capex. Headline CPI inflation increased sequentially, rising above the target during June-August, driven by a sustained positive price momentum. Food and fuel groups led to this increase, reflecting adverse weather conditions and the sharp rise in energy prices following the West Asia conflict. Core inflation registered a pick-up with some signs of generalisation in recent months. Input cost pressures have accentuated, but the pass-through has remained limited so far. Going forward, India’s macroeconomic outlook remains resilient supported by domestic demand and strengthening investment, despite persistent global uncertainties. The outlook remains vulnerable to geopolitical developments, volatility in global energy markets and weather-related uncertainties. Weak monsoons coupled with strong El Niño, protracted geopolitical tensions, rising international commodity prices, additional frictions in global trade and tightening of global financial conditions could adversely impact the growth outlook. Persistent supply-side pressures in food and volatile global energy prices pose risks to the domestic inflation outlook, particularly through second-round effects amid strong growth impulses. The interplay of these factors will shape the evolving growth–inflation dynamics, with the balance of risks depending on developments in global growth, crude oil prices, exchange-rate movements, and domestic food supplies. I. External Environment Global growth remains resilient, mainly supported by AI-related investment and fiscal measures, but faces renewed supply-side shocks from the West Asia conflict, elevated oil prices and trade related frictions. Inflation has accelerated again, prompting central banks to shift towards a more cautious and hawkish monetary policy stance. Financial markets remain volatile amid higher yields, geopolitical tensions and shifting risk sentiment. Global growth has remained resilient despite facing persistent headwinds from supply shocks. However, the near-term growth forecasts have been revised downwards by several multilateral agencies, as key supply chains remain disrupted and crude oil prices remain elevated. Investment in artificial intelligence (AI) and related technologies, along with increased international trade in AI-related hardware, has supported global economic activity. Fiscal support across countries has sustained economic activity but also heightened concerns about rising public debt and reduced fiscal buffers. Along with higher inflation and higher-for-longer monetary policy expectations, these concerns have contributed to a sharp rise in government bond yields across major jurisdictions. Inflation, which had been moderating towards the end of 2025, began to accelerate following the supply shock triggered by the West Asia conflict. Crude oil prices rose to levels not seen in recent years. At the same time, other commodity prices also increased, feeding into higher goods inflation even as services inflation remained elevated in several major economies. Consequently, central banks that had been moving towards monetary policy normalisation last year adopted a more hawkish stance following the onset of the conflict. Several advanced and emerging market economies (EMEs) have tightened monetary policy or maintained a cautious stance, while only a handful have reduced policy rates to support growth. Of late, the US Fed and the European Central Bank (ECB) have been placing greater emphasis on incoming data and their monetary policy frameworks in decision making, rather than on forward guidance. The Fed’s hawkish stance, combined with elevated crude oil prices, contributed to risk-off sentiment and portfolio outflows from EMEs, exerting depreciation pressure on their currencies. Sovereign bond yields have hardened globally, particularly in advanced economies (AEs), on concerns over rising public debt, debt-servicing costs and persistent inflation concerns. Emerging market equities experienced selloffs during Q3 of 2026, with some recovery in August while advanced economy equities gained, driven by technology stocks and healthy corporate profits. The US dollar gained, as higher bond yields, expectations of a hawkish Fed, and safe-haven demand amid geopolitical uncertainty outweighed intermittent weakness. I.1 Global Economic Conditions In 2026 so far, global growth has remained resilient, even as near-term growth forecasts have been revised downwards amid the fragile geopolitical situation in West Asia. The growth outlook is dependent on the de-escalation of the conflict, as key supply chains continue to face disruptions, and oil prices remain elevated. In its July 2026 World Economic Outlook update, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) lowered its global growth projection for 2026 by 10 bps to 3.0 per cent, reflecting the uncertainty around the outlook. However, it raised its projection by 20 bps for 2027 to 3.4 per cent, as the impact of the conflict remains less than what was anticipated earlier, while AI-related investment and productivity gains are likely to fuel growth. Meanwhile, the OECD, in its September 2026 Interim Economic Outlook, marginally raised its global growth forecast by 10 bps to 2.9 per cent for 2026, while lowering its 2027 projection by 10 bps to 3.0 per cent. While AI-related activity is expected to provide continued support, stronger price pressures and elevated interest rates are likely to weigh on near-term growth momentum. Among AEs, real GDP growth in the US remained resilient in 2026, supported by robust consumer spending and investment, including continued private investment in AI and related technologies. Growth, however, moderated in the second quarter, reflecting a downturn in government spending, slower investment and export growth, while stronger consumer spending partly offset these effects ( Table I.1 ). Since April 2026, labour market conditions have softened, with non-farm payroll growth slowing down during summer and weakening further in September, while the unemployment rate remained largely stable. The composite PMI continued to expand strongly in August, recording a 52-month high, driven by services while manufacturing remained healthy amid improved business optimism and new orders. Consumer sentiment, as measured by the University of Michigan Survey, declined in September to its lowest level in four months, amid growing concerns about elevated prices. Overall, underlying economic activity in the US remains resilient. Among other AEs, growth in Japan in 2026 so far has been largely driven by the external sector. GDP growth strengthened in Q1, with net exports making the largest contribution. Growth moderated in Q2 due to slowdown in domestic demand, particularly private investment, though this moderation was offset largely by a strong contribution from net exports. The composite PMI continued to expand in August, driven by manufacturing while services also improved. On the other hand, GDP growth recovered in the euro area in Q2 after stagnating in Q1, primarily driven by strong growth in Ireland and Spain. Household and government expenditure continued to provide support to economic activity. The composite PMI expanded in August at the same pace for the second consecutive month as the moderation in services was offset by solid expansion in manufacturing amid growth in new orders and factory output. In the UK, GDP growth rebounded in Q1 2026, supported by services and broad-based expansion across the economy, with gross capital formation and household consumption driving growth on the expenditure side. Growth moderated in Q2, reflecting weaker household consumption and lower inventory accumulation amid the adverse effects of the conflict in West Asia. Among high-frequency indicators, the composite PMI expanded in August for the second consecutive month, driven by services sector activity offsetting the moderation in manufacturing. Sources: Official statistical agencies; Bloomberg; and IMF. Among major EMEs, China’s growth is facing challenges from subdued consumption and a weaker external sector in 2026, with GDP growth moderating in Q2 from Q1. The composition of growth has also undergone a shift, with the share of net exports in GDP growth declining significantly relative to 2025, while the share of gross capital formation increased. Investment growth remains uneven, with stronger activity concentrated in AI-related and high-tech sectors. High-frequency indicators also point to subdued activity, with composite PMI slowing in July as both manufacturing and services sector activity moderated. In August, however, PMI rebounded as output and new orders increased in both the sectors but remained below the average for 2026. Brazil’s GDP growth remained stable at 1.8 per cent (y-o-y) in Q1, marking the third consecutive quarter of growth at this pace. The agriculture and services sectors supported growth while industrial activity declined. In Q2, however, GDP expanded by 2.0 per cent, driven by recovery in industrial sector and sustained growth in agriculture. Industrial sector benefited from higher oil and gas extraction amid higher energy prices. Brazil’s composite PMI remained very close to the neutral line in the last few months, reflecting weakness in the economy as new orders continue to fall. Russia’s economy contracted in Q1, reflecting weak manufacturing and construction activity, although services remained resilient. Activity recovered in Q2, led by manufacturing, while agriculture remained subdued. The composite PMI also returned to expansion in August, ending five consecutive months of contraction, supported by stronger output and new orders. In South Africa, GDP growth accelerated in Q1, driven by a recovery in agriculture, increased mining activity, and stronger momentum in services, before moderating in Q2 led by a contraction in manufacturing and mining. Composite PMI continued to remain around neutral line in August amidst subdued new orders and weak business confidence. The Asian Development Bank (ADB), in its September 2026 outlook, projected ASEAN 1 growth at 4.7 per cent in both 2026 and 2027. The outlook remains subject to downside risks from the West Asia conflict, elevated energy and commodity prices, weaker external demand and heightened global uncertainty. Turning to high-frequency indicators, the OECD’s composite leading indicators (CLIs) showed that most economies remained above their long-term trend in Q2 and Q3 (till August) of 2026 ( Chart I.1a ). The global composite PMI expanded at its quickest pace in August in more than two years, with broad-based expansion in both output and new orders ( Chart I.1b ). The services sector continued to expand in August for the fifth straight month, while the manufacturing sector remained solid. World merchandise trade expanded for eleven consecutive quarters through Q2:2026, with growth remaining robust and exceeding expectations. Both EMEs and AEs contributed to the expansion, though the impulse came largely from EMEs, with moderation in contribution by the AEs as frontloading of US imports moderated. In July 2026, world merchandise trade volume growth remained strong at 6.0 per cent (y-o-y), with EMEs contributing 3.2 percentage points and AEs 2.8 percentage points ( Chart I.2a ). The surge in trade of electronic components related to AI offset the negative impact of the conflict in West Asia. The WTO, in its March 2026 update, revised its projection for global merchandise trade volume growth from 0.5 per cent to 1.9 per cent in 2026, reflecting strong AI-related trade and a smaller-than-anticipated impact of tariffs. The Goods Trade Barometer (September 2026, WTO) remained above trend at 102.0, with the electronic components and other goods linked to investment in artificial intelligence (AI) indices indicating continued momentum in merchandise trade. Meanwhile, shipping costs remained elevated, with the Freightos Baltic Global Index staying higher in 2026 - above its 2025 average - reflecting the rerouting of vessels away from disrupted shipping corridors/chokepoints and continued capacity pressures ( Chart I.2b ). I.2 Commodity Prices and Inflation Commodity prices, as captured by the Bloomberg Commodity Index, have exhibited divergent movements, largely attributable to sector-specific fundamentals ( Chart I.3a ). Agricultural commodity prices have risen due to conflict-related disruptions to energy, fertiliser and shipping markets, adverse weather conditions and tighter crop-supply prospects. Global food prices, as reflected in the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) food price index, have increased since April 2026, mainly due to vegetable oils, cereals, and sugar ( Chart I.3b ). Gold prices declined through Q2 2026 amid expectations of higher interest rates. Gold prices gained overall in Q3 as heightened geopolitical uncertainty, including renewed tensions in West Asia, boosted safe-haven demand. Periods of weakness in the US dollar and lower expectations of further tightening by the Fed also supported prices, outweighing the drag from rising bond yields and the stronger dollar in September. Among base metals, copper and zinc prices have continued to rise, supported by tightening supply conditions. Aluminium prices rose to a four-year high in early June amid concerns over supply disruptions from the West Asia conflict, before moderating as the US dollar strengthened and Chinese exports increased ( Chart I.3c ). Energy prices surged in April, largely reflecting the sharp increase in Brent prices, before moderating as supply disruptions eased. However, the re-escalation of tensions in West Asia led to a renewed increase in energy prices in August and September, amid concerns over disruptions in regional oil production and shipping ( Chart I.4a ). Against this backdrop, developments in global oil supply buffers and demand conditions remain important. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) is currently placed at roughly 284 million barrels, at its lowest level since October 1982. Strategic releases and inventory drawdowns helped to cushion shocks. Also, weaker import demand by China due to release of stocks and domestic demand destruction helped offset some supply pressures. However, if the disruptions last longer, there is lower flexibility available to deal with supply shortages ( Chart I.4 b&c ). Consumer Price Inflation Inflationary pressures have re-emerged following a temporary moderation, driven primarily by renewed energy and commodity price pressures amid heightened West Asia tensions. The US personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation metric, saw inflation surge through May, driven by a sharp increase in gasoline prices before falling subsequently as energy prices stabilised. In the UK, headline inflation has been lower in Q2 2026, mainly due to easing food inflation, before edging up in Q3 so far on rising energy and housing prices. In the euro area, energy prices and persistently high service inflation drove the CPI inflation higher, except for a modest correction in June due to a reversal in crude prices. In Japan, inflation rose steadily from April, reflecting a slower decline in energy prices as subsidies were scaled back in Q2, alongside imported inflation from yen depreciation. Inflation rose further in Q3, on elevated food prices and transportation costs, despite lower electricity prices. In EMEs, inflation has been divergent, reflecting differences in domestic demand conditions and supply-side pressures across economies. In Brazil, the headline CPI rose due to food and beverages, then fell as food, transport, and housing prices moderated. Inflation in South Africa accelerated from April to June, driven predominantly by higher fuel and transport costs, before easing in July as fuel prices declined and food-price inflation moderated. In Russia, CPI inflation eased until May on easing food pressures before edging higher due to fuel and a weaker rouble. China’s CPI inflation has remained subdued, supported by persistent food-price deflation ( Chart I.5b ). I.3 Monetary Policy Stance Since April 2026, monetary policy actions have diverged across economies. However, major advanced economy central banks turned more hawkish in Q3 2026, as renewed West Asia tensions raised energy prices and intensified inflationary pressures. Among major AEs, the US Fed held the target range at 3.50–3.75 per cent through July. In September, amidst persistent inflationary pressures, robust economic activity and stable labour-market conditions, the Fed unanimously raised the target range by 25 basis points to 3.75–4.00 per cent. The Bank of England has maintained the policy rate unchanged at 3.75 per cent in the last six meetings, noting little evidence so far of material second-round effects from the energy shocks while reiterating that future policy decisions depend on how the energy shock evolves and its impact on inflation. The ECB raised its key policy rates by 25 basis points in June and again in September, taking the deposit facility rate to 2.50 per cent. The decisions reflected persistent energy-driven inflation pressures associated with the conflict; however, indirect and second-round effects have remained largely contained. The Bank of Japan (BoJ) continued policy normalisation, raising its policy rate by 25 basis points each in June and September to 1.25 per cent. The moves reflected persistent inflationary pressures, owing to higher import costs amid yen depreciation, with future policy decisions to be guided by developments in economic activity and prices. The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates in May amid elevated inflation and capacity pressures, and again in September as fuel-price pass-through and stronger-than-expected growth intensified inflation risks. The Bank of Canada maintained status quo as longer-term inflation expectations have remained anchored and there was little evidence that oil prices had fed through more broadly to goods and services prices. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand hiked the policy rate by 25 bps for the first time in three years in July and then again in September by the same magnitude to 2.75 per cent. The monetary policy committee considered gradual withdrawal of monetary stimulus as appropriate to steer inflation to the 2 per cent target, while supporting growth and employment ( Chart I.6a ). Among key EMEs, Brazil continued its monetary easing cycle, with the central bank reducing the Selic rate in successive meetings amid signs of moderating economic activity and easing inflationary pressures. The Bank of Russia has gradually reduced its key rate as economic growth edged lower. China has held its benchmark rate at 3.0 per cent for more than a year amid ample liquidity. South Africa raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 7.25 per cent in September, following a similar increase in May, amid rising inflation risks and concerns over potential second-round effects. The Bank of Thailand kept its policy rate unchanged, balancing weaker growth and subdued domestic demand against conflict-related, supply-driven inflation pressures. The Bank of Mexico cut its policy rate by 25 basis points to 6.5 per cent in May, marking the end of its easing cycle. In September, it kept rates unchanged but removed its earlier forward guidance, signalling greater policy flexibility ( Chart I.6b ). I.4 Financial Markets Global financial markets remained largely resilient yet volatile, guided by the interplay of AI-driven risk appetite, shifting monetary policy expectations, elevated sovereign borrowing needs, and persistent geopolitical tensions in West Asia. The stock-bond correlation in the AEs has shifted for the first time in decades, reflecting uncertainty due to supply-side shocks ( Box I.1 ). Box I.1: Stock–Bond Correlation in Advanced and Emerging Economies The equity–government bond return correlation is central to multi-asset portfolio diversification. Stock–bond return correlation is influenced by short-term rates, inflation, volatility, and economic growth (Aslanidis and Christiansen, 2012). Theoretical explanations link asset-price co-movement to macroeconomic conditions (Campbell et al., 2020), while changes in stock–bond correlation have important implications for portfolio diversification (Brixton et al., 2023). More recently, evidence from G7 economies suggests that the macroeconomic drivers of stock–bond correlation vary over time, with significant implications for portfolio risk and diversification (McMillan, 2026). After two decades of generally positive readings, the correlation in advanced economies turned sharply negative during the 2021–22 inflation surge and again in 2025 ( Chart I.1a ). Using a DCC-GARCH model, the analysis finds that stock–bond correlation in advanced economies follows an inflation-regime relationship. Inflation enters with a negative linear and positive quadratic term, implying that correlation is lowest near the inflation target and rises as inflation moves away from it ( Chart I.1b ). The implied turning point is 1.6 per cent, essentially at the 2 per cent target, and the real short rate is also positive and significant. The findings suggest that when inflation is moderate, government bonds tend to hedge equity-market risk. This mechanism, however, does not extend to emerging markets. Their correlation averages around +0.6 and never turns negative over the sample, while its relationship with domestic inflation is weak and statistically insignificant. A formal Wald test also rejects equality of the advanced- and emerging-market coefficients. Instead, global equity volatility (VIX) is the only significant explanatory variable. The results suggest that emerging-market government bonds behave more like risk assets than domestic safe havens, selling off alongside equities when global risk appetite deteriorates. Thus, their diversification benefits are not evident in the post-2008 sample, unlike in advanced economies. References: 1. Global equities advanced in Q2 2026, driven by continued momentum in artificial intelligence (AI) and related capital investment cycles ( Chart I.7a ). Geopolitical tensions in West Asia added sporadic volatility during the quarter. The announcement of a US–Iran ceasefire framework and a memorandum of understanding (MoU) eased concerns about a broader regional conflict. Energy prices recoiled, and investor sentiment improved as fears of a sustained disruption to global energy supplies diminished. During Q2, US equities advanced, supported by resilient corporate earnings and sustained investor enthusiasm for AI-related companies. In the euro area, equities posted solid gains, with IT outperforming amid strong corporate earnings and diversification by investors from US markets. In the UK, equity prices rose, although declines in energy stocks limited overall gains. Markets largely looked through domestic political developments, with investor sentiment remaining broadly resilient. Japanese equities delivered robust returns in Q2 as easing tensions in West Asia buoyed sentiment, while the yen – at a four-decade low against the US dollar – supported exporters. In Q3, major equity markets posted modest gains, although investor sentiment remained cautious amid expectations of further monetary tightening, elevated technology-sector valuations, and persisting tensions in West Asia. Equities gained in the US, supported by resilient corporate earnings and sustained AI optimism, with further support from the Fed’s commitment to combating inflation despite its hawkish stance. Euro-area equities declined in Q3 as higher energy prices and persistent inflation lifted bond yields and weighed on risk sentiment, while political uncertainty and fiscal concerns, added to investor caution. Japanese equities were affected by the global correction in AI-related stocks and also concerns surrounding a stronger yen which could weigh on exports. In the UK, equities made modest gains, supported by robust corporate earnings, and elevated commodity prices. Equity markets in most EMEs rose sharply in Q2:2026, outperforming global peers. Taiwan and Korea led market performance, driven by gains in memory and semiconductor stocks amid strong AI demand ( Chart I.7b ). In Q3, emerging-market equities surrendered the gains recorded in the previous quarter as the AI-led rally showed signs of fatigue. Renewed conflict in West Asia, heightened trade tensions, and expectations of a more hawkish Fed weighed on investor risk appetite. A global sell-off in government debt led by inflation persistence and high government deficits has raised borrowing costs. These pressures have been exacerbated by the West Asia conflict, which has driven up oil prices, leading investors to seek higher bond yields as the odds of rate cuts have largely diminished. Sovereign bond-market performance diverged in Q2: Japanese and US rates firmed up, while German and UK yields softened. Developments in West Asia continued to be a major driver of the market, with bond yields moving in tandem with oil prices. Yields on government bonds surged to multi-year highs around the middle of the quarter amid fears of further escalation but fell on signs of a possible US–Iran deal. In the US, rates were underpinned by a resilient labour market and elevated government debt, reinforcing expectations that monetary policy would remain tight. A combination of global inflation concerns, and domestic politics hit UK gilts. In April, the 10-year gilt yield hit its highest level since 2008, reflecting inflationary pressures from higher oil prices and concerns about budgetary and political vulnerabilities ahead of municipal elections. Higher oil costs and imported-inflation pressures from the yen supported expectations for BoJ policy hikes this year, while concerns about fiscal expansion contributed to upside pressure. In Q3, government bond yields in major AEs have risen amid persistent energy-price pressures and tighter monetary policy, while elevated public debt and renewed fiscal support have added to upward pressure on long-term yields. In the US, higher oil prices, persistent inflation concerns, and higher borrowing requirements pushed treasury yields higher. The Treasury’s decision in mid-August to expand buybacks of long-dated securities provided only temporary relief, as underlying inflation and term-premium pressures continued to weigh on the market. Elsewhere, government bond yields in the euro area, Japan and the UK moved up amid renewed inflation concerns from rising energy prices, while rate hikes and firm policy signals, along with country-specific fiscal risks and elevated sovereign borrowing requirements, added to the rise in yields ( Chart I.8 a ). Emerging-market 10-year sovereign bonds recorded a mixed performance, displaying divergent country-specific inflation, fiscal, and monetary policy dynamics. While favourable risk sentiment and easing expectations initially supported some markets, the subsequent rise in oil prices, US sovereign bond yields, and geopolitical tensions tightened external financing conditions, increasing borrowing costs and weighing more heavily on sovereigns vulnerable to fiscal and external risks ( Chart I.8b ). In currency markets, the US dollar strengthened in Q2 2026, supported by higher oil prices, heightened geopolitical tensions and still elevated inflation, which reinforced safe-haven demand and expectations of relatively tighter monetary policy. Most major currencies weakened against the US dollar, with the yen declining to a four-decade low despite large scale coordinated intervention by the US and the Bank of Japan. The euro also depreciated, while sterling demonstrated greater resilience. In Q3, the US dollar, which had remained broadly weak through much of the quarter, strengthened markedly in September. The rebound was driven by higher US bond yields and a repricing of expectations for further Fed tightening following the release of data suggesting resilient activity and persistent inflation concerns. Renewed geopolitical tensions in West Asia, elevated oil prices, and trade-related uncertainty also supported safe-haven demand for the dollar. Consequently, the dollar index rose by around 2.0 per cent during September to a near two-month high, although it ended Q3 only marginally higher. Against this backdrop, the renewed negative correlation between the S&P 500 and the US dollar since April indicates that the dollar has again provided a partial hedge during periods of equity-market stress, appreciating when risk sentiment deteriorated and weakening as risk appetite recovered ( Chart I.9 ). Shifts in monetary policy expectations, geopolitical developments, and global risk appetite can, however, quickly alter the stock–dollar correlation. The MSCI EM Currency Index rose driven by carry-seeking flows, supportive commodity prices and country-specific inflows. However, gains moderated late in the period amid renewed pressure from rising long-term US bond yields ( Chart I.10 a & b ). I.5 Conclusion The global economic outlook continues to be shaped by supply-side shocks emanating from the West Asia crisis, shifting trade tariffs, and the ongoing AI investment boom. Despite multilateral agencies projecting slower global growth in 2026, high-frequency indicators, including purchasing managers’ indices, point to resilient economic activity. Inflation has picked up in most economies, prompting central banks to adopt a more hawkish stance. Long-term bond yields have risen amid persistent inflation concerns, while equity markets have advanced, underpinned by the ongoing AI-driven investment boom. II. Liquidity Conditions and Financial Markets System liquidity surplus surged during H1:2026-27 mainly on account of the Reserve Bank’s swap facilities. Overnight rates in the money market evolved in sync with prevailing liquidity conditions. Domestic financial markets exhibited two-way movements amidst global uncertainty. Transmission to lending rates moderated with status quo on policy rate since February 2026. Bank credit growth accelerated further. Sectoral trends indicate broad-based credit expansion. Introduction Global financial markets remained volatile amidst shifting expectations, persistent tensions in West Asia and rising fiscal concerns. Against this backdrop, domestic financial markets displayed intermittent volatility during H1:2026-27. System-wide liquidity surplus surged in September 2026 reflecting buoyant capital flows under the Reserve Bank’s swap facilities. Money market rates largely moved in line with the evolving liquidity conditions, with rates in Certificates of Deposit (CDs) and Commercial Papers (CPs) easing in Q2. The exchange rate exhibited two-way movements in H1. Monetary policy transmission to lending rate moderated during H1 amidst rate pause and funding pressure. Nonetheless, bank credit continued to grow robustly and financing from non-bank sources also increased. II.1 Liquidity Conditions and the Operating Procedure of Monetary Policy The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Act, 1934 requires the Reserve Bank to place the operating procedure relating to the implementation of monetary policy and changes thereto from time to time, if any, in the public domain. 1 During H1:2026-27, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) kept the policy rate unchanged in three successive meetings while retaining the neutral policy stance. Drivers and Management of Liquidity System liquidity, as measured by the net balances under the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF), improved significantly in H1:2026–27 from a moderate surplus in H2:2025–26 ( Chart II.1 ). On a net basis, average daily absorption under the LAF increased to ₹3.21 lakh crore in H1:2026–27 from ₹1.43 lakh crore in H2:2025–26. Capital inflows and the build-up of government cash balances were the principal drivers of liquidity conditions in H1:2026–27. System liquidity remained in surplus during H1:2026-27 except for end-June when it briefly turned into deficit amidst tax related outflows. 2 In Q1, liquidity conditions improved initially supported by faster government spending, but it moderated thereafter due to increase in currency in circulation (CiC) and the RBI’s foreign exchange operations. Liquidity conditions improved in Q2, aided by capital inflows under the RBI's swap facilities ( Table II.1 ). With liquidity conditions remaining largely in surplus, banks’ recourse to the marginal standing facility (MSF) averaged ₹0.01 lakh crore during H1:2026-27, while average daily standing deposit facility (SDF) balances increased marginally 3 . The Reserve Bank remained nimble and agile in its liquidity management operations, ensuring sufficient liquidity in the banking system to support transmission to money market. With surge in liquidity surplus mainly due to FCNR(B) swaps 4 , the RBI conducted variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) operations of varying maturities, although several variable rate repo (VRR) operations were also undertaken mainly until July 2026 to tide over transient liquidity tightness and align overnight rates with the policy rate. Overall, the RBI conducted a total of 36 VRR and 51 VRRR auctions in H1. As on September 15, 2026, reserve money expanded by 8.5 per cent (y-o-y) as against 5.6 per cent a year ago. Adjusted for the first-round impact of CRR change, growth in reserve money stood at 11.9 per cent (9.4 per cent a year ago). The higher growth in reserve money was driven by expansion in currency in circulation.
