II.2 Domestic Financial Markets Money market rates softened in H1:2026-27 in tandem with evolving liquidity conditions. G-sec yields eased until August before hardening in September, reflecting higher global yields, rising oil prices, and expectations of monetary tightening. Corporate bond yields moved in sync with G-sec yields, with a hardening bias, while risk premia showed mixed trends. Equity markets gained marginally despite heightened volatility in global financial markets and crude oil prices due to West Asia conflict. The foreign exchange market remained volatile amid shifting US policies and lingering conflict in West Asia. In the credit market, both bank and non-bank credit grew at a robust pace. II.2.1 Money Market During H1:2026-27, money market rates softened and remained mostly range bound amid large surplus liquidity conditioned by robust capital inflows, especially from FCNR(B) deposits under the Reserve Bank’s swap facility announced in June 2026. The weighted average call rate (WACR) – the operating target of monetary policy – generally remained within the policy rate corridor. However, with the significant rise in surplus liquidity, it moved downward towards the SDF rate, floor of the corridor, in September ( Chart II.2a ). Volatility in the WACR, as measured by the exponential weighted moving average (EWMA) 6 , declined considerably in the beginning of FY 2026-27, however, it increased marginally in July, and remained moderate till September ( Chart II.2b ). Reflecting the evolving liquidity conditions, the average spread of WACR over the policy repo rate turned positive during May-July 2026, before turning negative in August and plunging further in September ( Chart II.2b ). Overnight rates in the collateralised segment, i.e., triparty repo (TREPS) and market repo, broadly tracked the WACR, although both fell below the SDF rate intermittently during H1:2026-27 ( Chart II.3 ). Money market activity remained concentrated in the collateralised segments (tri-party and market repo), with their share in overnight money market volume at 97 per cent. During H1:2026-27, the share of the uncollateralised segment, i.e., the call money market, persisted around 3 per cent. Mutual funds remained the major lenders in tri-party repo with their share unchanged at 65 per cent in H1:2026-27, while their share in total lending in market repo segment moderated to 41 per cent in H1 from 48 per cent in H2:2025-26. The share of foreign banks in market repo lending increased to 31 per cent in H1:2026-27 from 29 per cent in H2:2025-26. On the borrowing side, public sector banks (PSBs) were the major player in tri-party repo, with their share increasing to 35 per cent in H1:2026-27 from 32 per cent in H2:2025-26. The share of private banks reduced noticeably to 14 per cent from 24 per cent. The share of PSBs in market repo increased by 5 percentage points to 13 per cent over the same period. The rates in term segments of the money market also moved in line with the evolving liquidity conditions and uncertainty (also see Box II.1 ). While 3-month treasury bill (T-Bill) rates moved largely in line with the policy repo rate, the rates on certificates of deposits (CDs) and commercial papers (CPs) edged up in May, but moderated since July notwithstanding intermittent spikes. The average spread of CDs and CPs over the policy repo rate widened to 135 bps and 155 bps in H1:2026-27 from 116 bps and 136 bps, respectively, in H2:2025-26. The average spread of T-Bills over the policy repo rate increased to 5 bps from 1 bp over the same period ( Chart II.3 ). Box II.1: Drivers of CD and CP Rate Spreads Rates on short-term instruments like Certificates of Deposit (CDs) and Commercial Papers (CPs) generally move in tandem with the policy repo rate but diverge at times reflecting broader liquidity conditions and funding pressures. Starting from Q3 of 2025-26, CD/CP rates hardened and remained elevated even as the monetary policy easing cycle continued. It resulted in widening of spread of CD/CP rates over the policy repo rate. Besides liquidity conditions and funding pressures, several other factors can cause CP and CD spreads to deviate from their long-run averages, including, policy uncertainty, monetary policy expectations and market-specific factors such as issuance patterns, calendar effects, and episodes of market stress (Priyadarshini et al., 2024, Anshul et al., 2025). To disentangle the respective contribution of various factors which are intertwined and may operate simultaneously, uncorrelated shocks are identified using historical decompositions within a VAR framework using monthly data. The following VAR specification is used. Where Y t includes the selected endogenous variables, X t contains the exogenous dummies and Pε t are the orthogonalised shocks. The variables are selected to capture the main channels, viz., banking system liquidity, funding conditions and policy uncertainty through which they can affect short-term funding costs, while avoiding overlap across closely related measures. 7 For CDs, the funding block also captures banks’ balance-sheet pressures through changes in outstanding credit-deposit ratio and net CD issuance growth. For CPs, only net issuance growth is used to capture funding conditions. The uncorrelated shocks are identified using a recursive identification scheme where the most exogenous factors are placed at the top while the response variable, i.e., CD or CP spreads are placed at the end of the ordering. Historical decomposition for the period January 2025 – July 2026 show the extent of contribution by each identified factor to the movements in spreads ( Chart II.1.1 ). The decomposition results suggest that the drivers of CD and CP spreads have shifted over time. Relatively tight liquidity conditions were the main driver of widening spreads during early 2025, but increased system liquidity along with policy rate easing led spreads to moderate to relatively lower levels by mid-2025. Since late 2025, the spreads hardened again. Funding pressures, owing to stronger credit growth relative to deposit mobilisation, contributed to hardening of CD spread, while economic policy uncertainty was the main driver of widening CP spread. More recently, idiosyncratic market-specific pressures have also contributed to the widening which are unrelated to the identified shocks in the model. II.2.2 Government Securities Market Government securities (G-sec) yields experienced periodic bouts of volatility during H1:2026-27 due to challenging global environment and rise in global bond yields ( Chart II.6 ). In the wake of the West Asia conflict and a sharp rise in crude oil prices, G-sec yields remained elevated during April-May but softened generally in June-July as tensions in West Asia abated temporarily. Yields softened across the term structure during June-July 2026 as FPI debt flows improved after the announcement of special measures, including the expansion of the universe of Fully Accessible Route (FAR) securities by the Reserve Bank and tax concessions by the Government ( Chart II.7a ). After remaining range-bound in early August, the yields hardened again in September, owing to the rise in advanced economy yields, higher domestic inflation print and upward pressure on Brent crude oil prices following renewed West Asia tensions. Overall, the level of yield curve remained elevated during H1 ( Chart II.7b ). The average trading volume in G-secs increased in H1:2026-27 relative to H2:2025-26 ( Chart II.8 ). The weighted average yield on traded maturities for G-secs rose by 29 bps during the same period. As part of active debt consolidation, the Reserve Bank conducted six switch auctions of G-secs amounting to ₹1.1 lakh crore during H1:2026-27, on behalf of the Government of India. Furthermore, against the backdrop of an improved cash position, the Reserve Bank accepted offers totalling ₹25,704 crore through buyback auctions. The weighted average maturity (WAM) of the outstanding stock of G-secs increased from 13.70 years at end-March 2026 to 13.76 years as at end-September 2026, while its weighted average coupon (WAC) moderated from 7.17 per cent to 7.15 per cent over the same period. The weighted average spread of cut-off yields on State Government Securities (SGS) over G-sec yields of comparable maturities was 51 bps in H1:2026-27 as against 57 bps in H2:2025-26 ( Chart II.9 ). The average inter-state spread of cut-off yields on SGS of 10-year tenor (fresh issuances) was 6 bps in H1:2026-27 as against 12 bps in H2:2025-26. II.2.3 Corporate Bond Market Corporate bond yields evolved in sync with G-sec yields with a hardening bias during H1:2026-27, while the risk premia showed mixed trends ( Chart II.10a ). The average bond market risk premium (i.e., the spread of 3-year AAA corporate bond yields over 3-year G-sec yields) hardened from 129 bps to 140 bps for NBFCs, and from 112 bps to 122 bps for corporates, but remained stable at 109 bps for Public Sector Units (PSUs), Financial Institutions (FIs) and banks in H1, even as corporate earnings remained robust in Q1 ( Chart II.10b and Table II.4 ). Primary issuances of listed corporate bonds in domestic markets declined by 17.9 per cent during H1:2026-27 (up to August 2026) as compared to the corresponding period of the previous year reflecting higher yields ( Chart II.11a ). Overseas issuances increased to ₹1,31,931 crore during H1:2026-27 (up to August 2026) from ₹10,303 crore during the same period last year, partly attributed to RBI’s swap facility. Most of the resource mobilisation in the corporate bond market (99 per cent) was through the private placement route. Outstanding investments by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) in corporate bonds stood at ₹2.7 lakh crore as at end-September, 2026 with utilisation of investment limits at 29.3 per cent ( Chart II.11b ). Trading volume in the secondary market moderated to ₹9.5 lakh crore during H1 (up to August 2026) from ₹10.1 lakh crore during the corresponding period of the previous year. II.2.4 Equity Market During H1:2026-27, Indian equity markets gained despite heightened volatility in global financial markets and crude oil prices due to conflict in West Asia. Markets rebounded in April 2026 following the announcement of the US-Iran ceasefire. However, equity market remained subdued in May and early June as persistent tensions in West Asia, elevated crude oil prices and the IMD’s forecast of below normal monsoon weighed on investor sentiment. Thereafter, markets gained reflecting resilient corporate earnings results and a rebound in net buying by FPIs, even as the disruption of the US-Iran ceasefire reversed some gains in early July. Equity prices declined towards the end of August and early September amidst lingering geopolitical uncertainties, rising crude oil prices and higher global bond yields. II.2.5 Foreign Exchange Market The foreign exchange market remained volatile during H1:2026-27, driven by shifting US policies on tariff and policy rate, and lingering conflict in West Asia. While the rupee initially depreciated in the aftermath of the West Asia conflict, policy measures announced by the Reserve Bank and the Government to bolster capital flows arrested its decline. The implied volatility cooled down after peaking to a multi-year high in the wake of the West Asia conflict ( Chart II.15 ). Overall, the rupee depreciated by 1.4 per cent against the US dollar in H1:2026-27, a marked moderation from the sharp depreciation of 6.2 per cent witnessed in H2:2025-26 ( Chart II.16 ). The relative standing of the rupee among EM currencies also improved even as the pressures from volatile global market, elevated crude oil prices and the prolonged West Asia conflict weighed on the currency. Forward premia moderated during H1:2026-27 from the peak seen in the first week of April, supported by measures undertaken by the Government and the Reserve Bank to attract foreign capital. Upward pressures persisted, however, reflecting volatility in crude oil prices and flare-up of tensions in West Asia conflict ( Chart II.17 ). In terms of the 40-currency real effective exchange rate (REER), the INR depreciated by 0.5 per cent between March and August 2026, driven by the depreciation of the rupee in nominal terms ( Chart II.18a ). During the period, the movement in REER index was modest, as compared to major peer emerging economies ( Chart II.18b ). II.2.6 Bank and Non-Bank Credit Bank Credit: Aggregate Trends Bank credit growth strengthened further during H1: 2026–27 (up to September 15), on the back of robust loan demand ( Chart II.19 ). As on September 15, 2026, credit growth (y-o-y) for scheduled commercial banks (SCBs) accelerated sharply to 18.1 per cent, from 10.4 per cent during the corresponding period in the previous year ( Chart II.20 ). Across bank groups, foreign banks recorded the highest credit expansion at 25.8 per cent y-o-y, outperforming private banks (PVBs) at 19.1 per cent and public sector banks (PSBs) at 16.9 per cent. While PSBs contributed the largest share to y-o-y incremental credit, their overall market share contracted due to aggressive lending by both PVBs and foreign banks. The asset quality of SCBs strengthened further in Q1:2026-27 with the overall gross non-performing assets (NPA) ratio declining to 1.8 per cent in June 2026 from 2.3 per cent a year ago ( Chart II.21a ). The improvement spanned all major sectors, except for services and retail loans, where asset quality remained unchanged ( Chart II.21b ). Banks’ non statutory liquidity ratio (non-SLR) investments (comprising CPs, bonds, debentures, and shares of public and private corporates) increased by around 2.9 per cent during H1:2026-27 (up to September 15), with an increase in investments in commercial papers due to higher returns ( Chart II.22a ). Growth in adjusted non-food bank credit (i.e., non-food bank credit plus banks’ non-SLR investments) accelerated to 17.6 per cent (y-o-y) in Q2:2026-27 (up to September 15) from 10.1 per cent in Q2:2025-26, ( Chart II.22b ). As on August 31, 2026, excess holdings of SLR securities by SCBs marginally moderated to 6.3 per cent of their net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) from 6.4 per cent at end-March 2026 as banks brought down their investment portfolio to fund credit demand ( Chart II.23 ). Bank Credit: A Sectoral Perspective Sectoral trends 8 , 9 indicate strengthening of credit growth across major segments. Sustained robust economic activity continued to underpin credit demand, supporting broad-based expansion in bank credit. Monetary policy was found to have heterogenous impact on sectoral credit growth ( Box II.2 ). Box II.2: Bank Lending Channel of Monetary Policy: A Sectoral Approach Indian financial system continues to be bank-dominated. Bank credit as a proportion to GDP surged from 52.8 per cent in 2011-12 to 59.8 per cent in 2025-26. Therefore, given the importance of the banking sector, it becomes pertinent to understand the effectiveness of the transmission of monetary policy through the lending channel to various sectors of the economy. Under the current policy easing cycle, bank credit has inched up considerably across sectors. Demand conditions for credit have also been strong on the back of persisting buoyancy in domestic economic activity. In this milieu, it would be important to empirically decipher the response of sectoral bank credit to monetary policy shocks. Against this backdrop, the dynamic response of overall bank credit and credit to major sectors over 24 months following an unexpected policy rate change is examined using panel local projection technique (Jordà, 2005). Policy surprises are extracted using data on Overnight Index Swap (OIS) rates around RBI policy announcement dates, after controlling for current macroeconomic conditions (Lakdawala and Sengupta, 2025). Using monthly bank-level panel data of 40 banks for the period March 2014 - March 2026, the baseline specification for each horizon h = 0, 1, ..., 24 is given as under: Where, y i,t represents credit growth for bank i in time t, y i,t+h – y i,t–1 is the dependent variable representing the cumulative credit growth for bank i from the pre-shock period to horizon h, α i,h are bank fixed effects at horizon h, Shock t is the exogenous monetary policy (target factor) shock at time t, and β h is the coefficient of interest, capturing the cumulative impulse response of bank credit to a one standard deviation monetary policy shock at horizon h. Plotting β h for h = 0, 1, ..., 24 traces the impulse response function. Shock t–j are lagged shocks controlling for prior monetary policy actions, Δy i,t–j controls for lagged values of the dependent variable, credit growth, X i,t–1 is a vector of lagged bank characteristics (size, soundness, profitability, credit to deposits and borrowing ratio and asset quality) that can affect credit growth, MC t–p are lagged macroeconomic controls (nominal GDP growth and inflation) and D t and C t are dummies for demonetisation and COVID-19 pandemic, respectively. ε i,t+h is the idiosyncratic error term clustered at the bank level. The lag length (p) is set to 12 months following the documented 6-to-18-month transmission lag in the Indian banking sector (Khundrakpam and Jain, 2012; Raj, et al, 2020). The impulse response of aggregate non-food credit to a one standard deviation expansionary monetary policy shock indicates that credit expands over the short to medium term, increasing by approximately 0.50 percentage points (pp) within the first six months, peaking to 0.8 pp around 13 months after the shock but becomes insignificant by the 15th month. Credit growth increases immediately following expansionary monetary policy shocks, reaches a peak after one year, and gradually reverts as balance sheets adjust ( Chart II.2.1 ). Across major sectors, the impact of the expansionary monetary policy shock is found to be heterogeneous. Credit to agriculture sector remains steady initially, before expanding from around 4th month onwards, reaching the peak in around 18 months. Industry and services sectors respond immediately to the monetary policy shock, with industry reaching its peak expansion earlier (around 10 months) than services (around 13 months), after which both sectors’ responses gradually taper off. The response of personal loans is found to be delayed, remaining flat over the first few months, but it follows a steeper expansion and peaks around 10th month, like industry ( Chart II.2.2 ). Industrial credit growth also picked up and it was above its compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) over the last 10-year period in H1:2026-27, supporting overall credit expansion ( Table II.5 ). Services and personal loans continued to drive overall credit growth ( Chart II.24 ). Credit to industrial sector registered robust growth during H1:2026-27, largely attributable to a sharp acceleration in credit to large industries. This was supported partly by corporates’ reduced recourse to market-based funding as its cost was higher on account of heightened geopolitical tensions. Credit to MSMEs 10 continued on its double-digit growth trajectory, reflecting resilient credit demand including increased working capital requirements amidst global uncertainties and continued policy support. The policy support measures comprise the enhanced guarantee limit under the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE) scheme, Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) 5.0, among others ( Chart II.25 ). Among the major industrial sub-sectors, credit growth in infrastructure segment made a significant contribution to overall industrial credit expansion. 'Basic metal and metal products', ‘all engineering’ and 'chemicals and chemical products' also aided industrial growth ( Chart II.25b ). Within services sector, 'non-banking financial companies' (NBFCs) remained the largest recipient of bank credit during H1:2026-27, with improved availability following the withdrawal of the additional risk-weights effective April 1, 2025. Credit to services excluding NBFCs also expanded at a steady pace. Segments, such as trade and commercial real estate, recorded robust growth ( Chart II.26 ). Credit growth in personal loans segment remained buoyant during H1:2026-27, driven primarily by housing, loans against gold jewellery and vehicle loans. Housing loans, which account for nearly half of the personal loans, continued to grow at a steady pace reflecting robust real estate activity. Growth in loans against gold jewellery, albeit moderating from its peak in June 2025, remained elevated, which may be attributed to higher gold prices resulting in increased collateral valuation along with revised regulations effective from April 1, 2026 11 . Vehicle loan growth accelerated sharply, nearly doubling vis-à-vis the previous year, on the back of persistent demand following the GST cut ( Chart II.27 ). NBFC Credit: A Sectoral Perspective 12 Credit extended by NBFCs exhibited robust expansion since August 2025, driven primarily by strong retail credit. The marked acceleration in credit growth to segments such as housing and gold, coupled with steady credit expansion in vehicle loans, drove the buoyant expansion in retail credit. Industrial credit growth softened, reflecting a moderation in lending to infrastructure, especially power sector, during H1:2026-27 (up to August). Credit growth in services sector remain strong despite some deceleration in recent months vis-à-vis last year ( Table II.6 ). The continued buoyancy in retail lending underscored NBFCs' role in complementing the banking sector by catering to credit requirements of a diverse range of borrowers. At the same time, the weighted average lending rate (WALR) of banks have firmed up for fresh rupee loans, owing to strong credit demand. Bank credit growth outpaced deposit growth, leading to increased funding pressure. During H1 (till August), the WALR on fresh rupee loans increased by 21 bps, while it declined modestly by 3 bps for outstanding loans. In response to a cumulative reduction of 125 bps in the policy repo rate during February 2025 to August 2026, the WADTDRs for fresh and outstanding deposits have declined by 95 bps and 53 bps, respectively. On the lending side, WALRs for fresh and outstanding loans have declined by 72 bps and 91 bps, respectively. The share of the external benchmark-based lending rate (EBLR) linked loans in total outstanding floating rate loans of scheduled commercial banks increased from 67.6 per cent as at end-March 2026 to 68.2 per cent at end-June 2026. Consequently, the share of MCLR-linked loans declined from 30.2 per cent to 29.6 per cent. Public sector banks (PSBs) still have a significant proportion of their loans linked to MCLR ( Chart II.28a ), while private banks (PVBs) extend a large part of their loans at EBLR ( Chart II.28b ). The MCLR and other legacy rates – based on internal benchmarks and with longer reset periods – act as an impediment to faster policy transmission. PSBs have a high share of MCLR-linked loans in agriculture, infrastructure, other personal loans and large industry ( Chart II.29a ). The shares of MCLR-linked loans are lower for PVBs than those in PSBs ( Chart II.29b ). Bank group-wise, the transmission to WALRs on fresh and outstanding rupee loans of PVBs was higher than that of PSBs ( Chart II.30a ). The large share of EBLR-linked loans may have facilitated higher transmission in case of PVBs compared to PSBs. However, lending rates of PVBs remained above those of PSBs ( Chart II.30b ). The maximum pass-through to lending rates was witnessed among foreign banks, reflecting their higher share of EBLR-linked loans 13 and a higher share of low-cost bulk deposits of lower maturity. Sectoral analysis shows that the transmission to lending rates has been heterogeneous due to varying proportions of credit portfolios linked to fixed and floating interest rates and differential spreads charged by banks. Furthermore, the shifts in volumes across banks/sectors towards higher/lower interest rate slabs could impact aggregate lending rates. The WALRs showed a broad based decline across sectors since February 2025. The volume effect, however, partially dampened transmission in other personal loans and trade in fresh loans, whereas it complemented in sectors such as agriculture and education, thereby enhancing transmission ( Chart II.31 ). For EBLR-linked loans, PVBs have increased their spreads (charged over the repo rate) for education, housing, MSMEs and vehicle loans, which dampened the extent of transmission ( Table II.8 ). On the other hand, PSBs have reduced spread in education, MSME and vehicle loans, and increased it in other personal loans. For domestic banks, spread was higher in August 2026 over January 2025 for all sectors except education and vehicle loans. Through their extensive outreach and specialised lending activities across sectors, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) substantially contribute to the transmission of monetary policy via the credit channel. Nevertheless, NBFCs typically charge higher lending rates compared to SCBs, mainly due to differences in the risk profile of borrowers, their funding structures, and cost of liabilities. During February 2025 to August 2026, lending rates of NBFCs moderated across sectors. The highest transmission in fresh lending rates was recorded in advances against gold followed by vehicle and MSME loans ( Chart II.32 ). The Government of India reviewed the interest rates on various small savings instruments, which are linked to secondary market yields on G-secs of comparable maturities, and kept them unchanged for Q3:2026-27, marking 11 consecutive quarters with no change in rates. This has led to substantial positive spread of small saving instrument rates over their formula-based rates except for public provident fund ( Table II.9 ). The widening gaps may be limiting the transmission of policy rates to banks’ deposit rates, especially during policy easing, because of the potential substitution effect. A large interest rate differential in favour of small savings could lead to migration of deposits away from banks, thus widening the credit-deposit gap in the banking system. II.4 Conclusion Financial markets conditions remained largely congenial during H1:2026-27, with intermittent bouts of volatility arising from geopolitical uncertainties, fluctuations in crude oil prices and capital flows. System liquidity remained in surplus for most of the period, aided by capital inflows under the Reserve Bank’s special swap facilities. Money market rates softened and remained largely range bound in line with the evolving liquidity conditions. Government bond yields softened before hardening in September, mainly reflecting global developments. Corporate bond yields moved in tandem with G-sec yields. Domestic equity markets gained in H1, supported by robust corporate earnings, and renewed buying by foreign investors. The Indian rupee experienced two-way movements with a depreciating bias, although the pace of depreciation moderated. Bank credit growth remained robust and broad-based across major sectors. The non-bank sources of finance also expanded. Transmission to deposit rates further strengthened in H1, while it moderated in the case of lending rates. Going ahead, liquidity management operations will be conditional on evolving domestic financial conditions, monetary policy decisions and the stance of monetary policy. III. Demand and Output Domestic economic activity exhibited resilience in H1:2026-27, despite continued global uncertainty. Real GDP posted a strong growth of 7.8 per cent in Q1:2026-27. Private final consumption remained healthy, supported by buoyant discretionary consumption. Revival in private capex and government’s continued focus on infrastructure spending strengthened investment activity. Manufacturing expanded at a robust pace, while services sector maintained its buoyancy. Looking ahead, weak monsoons, the prolonged West-Asia conflict, additional frictions in global trade and tighter global financial conditions may have an adverse bearing on both the demand and supply side of the economy. Domestic economic activity exhibited resilience in H1:2026-27, despite continued global uncertainty amidst the prolonged West-Asia conflict. The supply-side pressures were effectively dealt with proactive policy measures that ensured supply of key inputs for productive sectors. As per the National Statistics Office (NSO)’s estimates, real GDP recorded a growth of 7.8 per cent in Q1:2026-27 reflecting strong momentum in underlying economic activity. Aggregate demand remained strong on the back of both private consumption and investment. Net external demand also contributed positively to growth with rebound in merchandise exports and sustained buoyancy in services exports. On the supply side, both manufacturing and services sectors recorded strong growth in Q1. Going ahead, weak monsoon and El Niño may weigh on agricultural activity. Industry and services sectors are expected to continue benefitting from the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme 5.0 and the Transition Facilitation (Quality Control) Order 2026. Similarly, India’s growing network of bilateral free trade agreements (FTAs) augurs well for external demand, though uncertainties about additional tariffs on US imports, including those under Section 301, pose some risk. The risks from protracted West Asia conflict and financial market repricing due to changes in US monetary policy also require close monitoring. III.1 Aggregate Demand Aggregate demand conditions in the economy held up well in Q1:2026-27. As per the statistics released by the National Statistics Office, real GDP grew by 7.8 per cent, up from 6.9 per cent a year ago. Despite modest rise in domestic prices of select commodities, private final consumption expenditure (PFCE) remained healthy, while double-digit growth in gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) suggests a strong recovery in the capex cycle ( Table III.1 ). Private final consumption contributed almost half of GDP growth in Q1:2026-27, though lower than 54.6 per cent a year ago. Strong growth in gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) also led to a sharp rise in its contribution to growth. By contrast, the contribution of government final consumption expenditure moderated in Q1. As real imports contracted and real exports rose sharply, net external demand was a positive contributor to GDP growth for the second successive quarter in Q1 ( Table III.1 and Chart III.1a ). The momentum of GDP – quarter-on-quarter (q-o-q) seasonally adjusted annualised growth rate (SAAR) – was placed at 6.5 per cent in Q1 ( Chart III.1b ). III.1.1 Private Final Consumption Expenditure Private consumption growth in Q1:2026-27 remained strong at 7.1 per cent compared to 6.8 per cent during the same quarter last year, supported by buoyant discretionary spending. The rising purchasing power of households, buoyed by a prolonged phase of low inflation, stable employment conditions, tax rationalisation, and robust rabi production in previous quarters bolstered households' discretionary spending. Among major high frequency indicators, passenger vehicle sales recorded double-digit growth in April-July 2026. Demand for consumer durables increased at a healthy pace in Q1 and July-August, while growth in consumer non-durables remained subdued. The non-housing retail loans, which generally support discretionary spending, also increased at a robust pace. Slowdown in domestic air passenger traffic since February 2026 reflected price pressures amid the West Asia conflict. Tractor sales expanded at a robust pace during April-July, before remaining flat in August, which coupled with buoyant growth in two-wheeler sales during April-August, imply strong rural demand conditions. However, the increase in demand for work under the Viksit Bharat–Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) [earlier MGNREGA] in August- September 2026 due to weakening of agricultural activity reflects a shift of rural households towards low-paying jobs ( Table III.2 ). The extent of pass-through of input costs, impact of weak monsoon on rural income, and continued momentum in manufacturing and service sector activities will remain pivotal to the sustenance of overall PFCE growth. Government’s policy measures to support agriculture, resilient agriculture allied sectors, and a wider fiscal safety net through direct benefit transfers may help protect rural income and consumption. III.1.3 Government Consumption Government final consumption expenditure (GFCE) in real terms grew by 4.3 per cent (y-o-y) in Q1:2026-27 compared to 7.7 per cent in the previous quarter ( Table III.1 ). Expenditure on major subsidies (comprising food, fertiliser, and petroleum) of the Centre registered a double-digit growth of 24.4 per cent during April-August 2026 3 led by expansion in fertiliser and food subsidy. Interest payments by the Centre, however, contracted during April-August 2026, over the corresponding period of 2025-26. Capital expenditure of the Centre registered a y-o-y growth of 18.2 per cent during April-August 2026 ( Chart III.5a ). Accordingly, the quality of government expenditure improved as the ratio of revenue expenditure to capital outlay (RECO) declined in April-August 2026, boding well for infrastructure-led development 4 ( Chart III.5b ). III.1.4 External Demand Amidst the ongoing West Asia crisis and lingering trade policy uncertainty, global demand conditions continue to remain fragile. Strong demand for AI-related goods and the frontloading of consumer goods in anticipation of additional US tariffs after the expiration of temporary tariffs in July 2026 9 , however, supported international trade. India's merchandise exports also rebounded and grew by 17.8 per cent in H1:2026-27 (April-August). With merchandise imports growing at a higher pace than exports, the merchandise trade deficit expanded to US$147.1 billion in H1:2026-27 (April-August) from US$ 123.9 billion in H1:2025-26 (April-August) ( Chart III.10 ). Improvement in export performance was broad-based as the share of commodity groups with double-digit growth in H1:2026-27 (April-August) was 73.4 per cent vis-à-vis 16.2 per cent in H1:2025-26 (April-August). Petroleum products; engineering goods; electronic goods; organic and inorganic chemicals; and meat, dairy and poultry products were the main drivers of merchandise exports growth. Exports to the US remained resilient, primarily driven by electronic goods and engineering goods. Sectors that were a drag on exports included readymade garments of all textiles; ceramic products and glassware; fruits and vegetables; tobacco; and spices ( Chart III.11a and b ). The growth in merchandise imports during H1:2026-27 (April-August) was driven by higher imports of electronic goods; petroleum, crude and products; machinery, electrical and non-electrical; fertilisers, crude and manufactured; and non-ferrous metals. By contrast, chemical material and products; pearls, precious and semi-precious stones; iron and steel; silver; and pulp and waste paper contributed negatively to import growth ( Chart III.12 ). Gold imports at US$ 17.5 billion grew by 3.4 per cent during this period, while petroleum, crude and products imports grew by 22.4 per cent to US$ 95.6 billion, both reflecting the value impact due to steep rise in prices. Despite elevated trade uncertainty, both net terms of trade and income terms of trade improved in Q1:2026-27 vis-à-vis Q4: 2025-26, implying greater purchasing power of exports in terms of imports. As prices of key imports softened in June, net terms of trade in Q1 recouped from losses in the previous quarter ( Chart III.13 ). India’s services exports growth remained robust at 10.9 per cent (y-o-y) in April-August 2026, led by software and business services ( Chart III.14 ). India remains one of the top five service-exporting countries worldwide in terms of export growth in Q1:2026-27. Services imports also registered a strong growth in April-August 2026 on the back of higher transport and business services. Net services surplus increased by 7.3 per cent to US$ 85.8 billion in April-August 2026. Despite significant widening of the goods trade deficit, the current account deficit (CAD) at US$ 4.2 billion (0.5 per cent of GDP) in Q1:2026-27 was marginally higher than its level of US$ 3.4 billion (0.4 per cent of GDP) in Q1:2025-26 ( Chart III.15 ). Services and remittance receipts continued to support the current account. There were net capital outflows of US$ 3.9 billion in Q1, as against net inflows of US$ 7.9 billion last year. 10 Consequently, India’s foreign exchange reserves depleted by US$ 8.1 billion (BoP basis) during the quarter. As per preliminary estimates, CAD widened to US$ 7.0 billion in July 2026 from US$ 3.2 billion a year ago, driven by higher merchandise trade deficit and net income outgoes. India’s gross inward foreign direct investment (FDI) and net FDI flows were higher in April-August 2026, both on y-o-y as well as sequential basis. A slowdown in the pace of outward FDI along with sustained higher gross FDI inflows supported net FDI flows. Financial services, communication services, computer services and manufacturing accounted for around 73 per cent of total FDI equity inflows during April-August 2026. In terms of origin, Singapore, Japan, Mauritius, The United Arab Emirates and the US were major sources of inward FDI to India, accounting for around 81 per cent of total inflows. Foreign portfolio investment (FPI) registered net outflows of US$ 8.9 billion during 2026-27 (up to September). After recording sustained outflows during the first quarter following geopolitical tensions in Middle East, FPI turned positive during June-August 2026 supported by measures taken by the RBI and the Government ( Table III.8 ). FPI flows reversed again in September 2026 amidst rising global risk-off sentiment on re-escalation of Middle East tensions and rising US bond yields. External commercial borrowing (ECB) agreements during April-August 2026 (P) increased significantly by 93.4 per cent (y-o-y) to US$ 30.4 billion, partly attributed to the RBI’s concessional US dollar-rupee swap facility introduced in June 2026 11 . Consequently, net ECB inflows to India 12 grew by 55.9 per cent to US$ 7.3 billion during April-August 2026 from US$ 4.7 billion a year ago. In terms of utilisation, on-lending/ sub-lending accounted for the highest share (28.0 per cent), followed by general corporate purpose (13.8 per cent) and refinancing of rupee loans (11.9 per cent) during this period. As at end-August 2026, about 73.0 per cent of outstanding ECBs (excluding rupee and inter-company borrowings) were hedged by the Indian companies. Net inflows under non-resident deposits stood at US$ 119.2 billion during April-August 2026 (P), significantly higher than US$ 5.6 billion a year ago due to a surge in FCNR(B) deposits on account of RBI’s forex swap facility. During June 8 - August 31, 2026, gross inflows under the FCNR(B) deposit scheme stood at US$ 133.0 billion 13 . As of September 25, 2026, India’s foreign exchange reserves stood at US$ 747.6 billion which is equivalent to 10.9 months of goods imports and 96.1 per cent of the external debt outstanding as at end-June 2026. III.2 Aggregate Supply Aggregate supply – measured by real Gross Value Added (GVA) at basic prices – expanded by 8.2 per cent in Q1:2026-27 (8.7 per cent in the preceding quarter) despite headwinds after the onset of the West Asia conflict. Proactive measures undertaken by the Government to ensure adequate supply of key inputs supported growth in both manufacturing and services sectors ( Chart III.16a and Table III.9 ). Supply-side measures included prioritisation of domestic supply and inventories, diversification of import sources of key inputs and targeted interventions to support the most vulnerable sectors. Some of these measures were subsequently withdrawn as supply-side pressures began to ease by end of Q1. The seasonally adjusted momentum of GVA moderated in Q1:2026-27 from the previous quarter ( Chart III.16b ). III.2.1 Agriculture Real GVA in agriculture and allied activities grew by 3.6 per cent in Q1:2026-27, lower than a year earlier. Robust growth in allied activities supported the overall growth in this sector. The shortfall and regional unevenness of Southwest monsoon and El Niño effects may pose some risks to both kharif and rabi output, though non-farm rural activities have shown greater resilience in recent years ( Box III.1 ). The Southwest monsoon, after remaining weak in June, gained significant momentum subsequently, covering the entire country by July 9, 2026. Monsoon remained 1.0 per cent above the long period average (LPA) in July and supported kharif sowing. As of September 30, 2026, the cumulative rainfall was 12.6 per cent below the Long Period Average ( Chart III.17a ). In terms of spatial distribution, rainfall remained deficient compared to the LPA across all regions. As of September 30, 2026, the production-weighted rainfall index (PRN) stood at 90 per cent, suggesting a skewed rainfall distribution in major crop producing states ( Chart III.17b ). As of October 1, 2026, reservoir levels at 71.8 per cent remained below normal level 14 (81.8 per cent) and last year’s level (90.3 per cent), due to erratic monsoon ( Chart III.17c ). Box III.1: Indian Agricultural Sector amidst Weather Shocks Rainfall shortfalls remain a major driver of year-to-year fluctuation in agricultural output. However, the rural economy is increasingly cushioned from erratic monsoon by resilient allied sector activities. Chand and Singh (2026) observe that for agricultural households possessing land up to one acre, wages contribute more than 55 per cent of household income, while crop production and livestock together contribute 36 per cent. This suggests that rural household incomes are increasingly supported by activities beyond crop production. Although annual estimates of value added are not available separately for rural and urban areas, historical benchmark estimates support the use of a broad rural-linked proxy. In 1999-2000, agriculture, forestry and fishing, mining and quarrying, and construction together accounted for about 59 per cent of total rural net domestic product (Central Statistical Organisation, 2007). This exercise therefore uses the sum of GVA of these sectors as an indicative proxy for rural-linked activity. Data available for both base years (i.e., 2011-12 and 2022-23) suggest that the non-agricultural component has become more important over time ( Chart III.1.1 ). The growth-rate analysis below is calculated within the relevant published GVA base, with 2023-24 onward using the 2022-23-base series. Rainfall sensitivity differs across the two components of the proxy, viz., agricultural and non-agricultural ( Chart III.1.2a ). Agricultural growth suffers more in years of higher monsoon deficit, while growth in the non-agricultural component stays close to 6 per cent at every cut-off. In years of surplus rainfall, by contrast, agricultural growth averages 5.1 per cent, above the 4.3 per cent recorded in years close to the LPA. It is estimated that non-agricultural activity was the predominant contributor to growth in rural economic activity during years of rainfall deficiency exceeding 7 per cent, as against in other years. The same contrast is evident in the regression estimates ( Chart III.1.2b ). Over 1994-95 to 2025-26, a regression of annual growth of agriculture and allied activities on the rainfall shortfall from the long-period average gives a coefficient of (–) 0.40, statistically significant at 1 per cent. The shortfall measure explains about 39 per cent of the variation in agricultural growth. For the non-agricultural component, the coefficient is 0.01 but not statistically significant ( Chart III.1.2b ). The pattern is also stable across two equal sub-periods. Including a separate term for rainfall above the LPA leaves the shortfall coefficient for agriculture largely unchanged at (–)0.44, while the excess-rainfall term is small and not statistically significant at (–)0.12. A formal test rejects a symmetric response to deficient and surplus rainfall for agriculture (p value = 0.04) but not for the non-agricultural component. The asymmetry is not an artefact of the censoring implicit in the shortfall measure. The evidence on the declining role of rainfall in crop production is in line with Gupta et al. 2023. The factors that seem to have reduced the sensitivity of agricultural activity to rainfall shortfall include increased irrigation coverage, new weather resilient crop varieties, and diversification towards less water-intensive crops. At the same time, the composition of agricultural output has shifted towards allied activities. Over 1999-2000 to 2024-25, the coefficient for agriculture and allied GVA is (–)0.44 and significant at 1 per cent while the coefficients for milk, eggs, meat and fish as well as non-agricultural component are small and statistically insignificant ( Chart III.1.3a ). These estimates suggest that growth in these activities is less closely related to aggregate rainfall shortfalls than agricultural GVA. Rolling correlations of the absolute deviation of rainfall from the LPA with growth in agricultural GVA and the rural-linked activity proxy have generally become less negative since the mid-2000s (irrespective of the window-length), while remaining below zero throughout ( Charts III.1.3b ). Summing up, empirical findings suggest that while rainfall shortfalls remain important for agricultural output, their association with allied activities and other rural-linked activity has moderated over time. Diversification across rural-linked activity and within agriculture has made the rural economy more resilient to rainfall shortfall. References: Chand, R., and J. Singh (2026). “Agriculture for Viksit Bharat: Strategies for Sustainable Growth and Transformation.” ICRIER Working Paper 434, July. Gupta, Kashyap; Sunil Kumar and Sarthak Gulati (2023), “Agriculture’s Dependency on Monsoon Rainfall in India”, RBI Bulletin, August. III.3 Conclusion Strong real GDP growth in Q1:2026-27, amidst global uncertainty and supply-side disruptions, signifies the inherent strength of the economy on the back of sustained focus on structural reforms, proactive policy responses, resilient macroeconomic fundamentals, and buoyant domestic demand. High frequency indicators available for Q2 suggest continued buoyancy in domestic economic activity, albeit with some moderation compared to Q1. Stable employment conditions, continued positive impact of tax rationalisation, congenial financial conditions, revival in corporate investment, and a pickup in goods exports are expected to support economic activity going forward. While a double-digit growth in GFCF reflects improving investment sentiment, sustenance of private consumption growth will be vital to broad-based recovery in private capex. Going forward, weak monsoons coupled with strong El Niño, protracted geopolitical tensions, rising international commodity prices, additional frictions in global trade and tightening of global financial conditions could adversely impact the outlook. _________________________________________________________________________________ 1 Share of regular salaried employees increased from 25.5 per cent in Q4:2025-26 to 26.2 per cent in Q1:2026-27. IV. Prices and Costs Headline CPI inflation increased sequentially, rising above the target during June-August driven by a sustained positive price momentum. Higher food and fuel inflation led to this increase, reflecting adverse weather conditions and the sharp rise in energy prices following the West Asia conflict. Core inflation registered a pick-up with signs of generalisation in recent months. Going ahead, persistent supply-side pressures in food and volatile global energy prices pose risks to the domestic inflation outlook, particularly through second-round effects amid strong growth impulses. IV.1 Introduction The headline consumer price index (CPI) inflation 1 has been increasing steadily in the period since the release of the previous MPR in April 2026. From 3.4 per cent in March 2026, headline inflation increased over successive months to 4.4 per cent in June (the first print above the inflation target in seventeen months) and further to 4.8 per cent in August ( Chart IV.1a ). The sequential pick-up in inflation witnessed since March was driven by a strong price momentum, which more than offset the favourable base effects in each month ( Chart IV.1b ). 2 The momentum has been particularly strong since May. Among the major sub-components, food and fuel recorded sharp increases in y-o-y inflation over March levels ( Chart IV.2a ). Reflecting this, the contribution of food and fuel sub-components to headline inflation increased significantly ( Chart IV.2b ). The pick-up in food inflation was driven by unfavourable weather conditions and increasing fuel prices brought about by the sharp upturn in global energy prices following the West Asia conflict. Core inflation (CPI excluding food and fuel) also registered a pick-up, albeit by a lower magnitude upto July, reflecting limited pass-through of supply side pressures. In August core inflation accelerated to 4.2 per cent. The April MPR projections had factored in risks from the West Asia conflict and adverse weather conditions as part of the baseline forecast. Reflecting this, the actual inflation outcomes remained broadly in line with the projections ( Chart IV.3 ). 3 Inflation for Q2:2026-27 so far (July-August) has turned out to be about 20 basis points (bps) higher than the quarterly average projection, as food price pressures have accentuated in recent months. The remainder of the chapter delves deeper into component-wise developments in inflation, statistical properties of observed inflation trends as well as determinants of inflation. IV.2 Developments across Major Components of the CPI CPI Food and Beverages Food and beverages inflation increased from 3.7 per cent in March to 5.7 per cent in August 2026, driven by items other than vegetables ( Chart IV.4 ). Of the 200-bps increase in food inflation in August over March, nearly 48 per cent was contributed by two sub-components, viz., animal protein 4 and spices 5 , which together have a weight of about 36 per cent within the food and beverages division. The increase in inflation in animal protein primarily reflected rising input costs ( Chart IV.5a ). Higher feed and fodder costs, high transportation and packaging outlays, elevated energy prices, and heatwave-induced bird mortality contributed to the firming up of prices ( Chart IV.5b ). Inflation in spices rose steadily since January 2026 and touched 13.0 per cent in August, after being in deflation for a prolonged period. 6 Ginger, dry chillies and coriander contributed the most to the increase. The emergence of El Niño conditions and deficient southwest monsoon have raised risks to overall food price outlook. However, robust domestic production in the previous year, comfortable foodgrain stocks 7 , conducive trade policy measures and proactive supply management provided some cushion, keeping the cumulative price build-up so far broadly in line with that of non-El Niño years ( Chart IV.6 ). Among the major products, inflation in cereals and products 8 increased to 2.8 per cent in August 2026 from -0.2 per cent in April amidst a pickup in rice prices on account of lower kharif sowing ( Chart IV.7a ). The build-up in cereals prices during 2026-27 (up to August) has also been above the historical average ( Chart IV.7b ). Pulses 9 recorded a modest increase in y-o-y inflation, largely reflecting unfavourable base effects after remaining in deflation through most of 2025-26. Imports of key pulses from Myanmar, Brazil and Australia, along with government interventions in retail markets, helped keep prices at moderate levels. 10 Inflation in oils and fats was lower at 7.8 per cent by August 2026 as compared to over 20 per cent a year ago ( Chart IV.8a ). Despite the moderation, elevated global edible oil prices amid increased diversion towards biofuel production in major producing economies continue to pose pressure on domestic prices. Domestically, tighter mustard seed arrivals amid steady export demand also kept mustard oil prices elevated ( Chart IV.8b ). However, reduction in basic import duty on crude palm, soybean and sunflower oils is likely to soften domestic prices. 11 Vegetables 12 inflation remained moderate, averaging 3.5 per cent (y-o-y) in H1:2026-27 so far (April-August 2026), supported by improved production and robust market arrivals. 13 The price build-up in the Tomato, Onion and Potato (TOP) category was broadly aligned with its historical seasonal pattern while the increase in non-TOP vegetable prices remained below that observed in both El Niño and non-El Niño years ( Chart IV.9 ). The impact of the deficient 14 and uneven spatial rainfall distribution and lower kharif sowing 15 on food prices is reflected in the recent high frequency retail price data in certain food items such as sugar and onion. Sugar 16 prices increased by about 34 per cent since the first week of July to reach ₹65/ kg by late August, due to lower than anticipated domestic production, lower carry-over stocks, and precautionary stocking by market intermediaries 17 ( Chart IV.10 ). The government undertook targeted measures such as export restrictions, stock limits on dealers and bulk consumers, duty-free imports of up to 10 lakh tonnes of raw sugar, physical verification of stocks, and advancing the sugarcane crushing season to augment domestic availability and contain speculative pressures. Prices have since retreated in September. Onion prices have increased by about 84 per cent since end-June (up to September 30) due to depletion/ some spoilage of stored rabi stocks and concerns over the timing and quality of kharif arrivals amid uneven rainfall ( Chart IV.11 ). Although onion prices exhibit a seasonal uptick during August-September before the arrival of the kharif crops, the magnitude of increase has been much higher this year than the historical average. CPI Fuel Global crude oil prices ratcheted up since March 2026 along with an increase in the premium for refined products on account of extreme market tightness ( Chart IV.12 ). Reflecting the partial pass-through of this increase, CPI fuel 18 inflation went up from 0.4 per cent in April to 5.2 per cent in August. Among household fuel items included in CPI, domestic liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices were revised upwards by ₹60 per cylinder in early March 2026 and by a further ₹29 per cylinder in June, resulting in a cumulative increase of around 10.3 per cent. Kerosene and other fuel items also witnessed an increase in prices. Electricity prices, however, recorded a decline on a y-o-y basis on account of reduction in tariffs and provision of free or subsidised electricity in certain states (C hart IV.13a ). Within transport fuel, retail prices of petrol and diesel were increased in four successive rounds during the month of May leading to a 7.5 per cent increase for petrol and 8.4 per cent for diesel ( Chart IV.13b ). The magnitude of domestic price increases was however moderate as compared to the increase in global prices ( Chart IV.14 ). Part of the shock was absorbed by the Government by reducing the Special Additional Excise Duty on petrol and diesel by ₹10 per litre each in March to ease the burden on domestic consumers. After the initial surge, global oil prices have remained highly volatile with sharp two-way movements triggered by geopolitical developments. Amidst renewed uncertainty about the US-Iran negotiations, Indian basket crude oil prices increased from US$82 per barrel in July to around US$116 per barrel in September. 19 Tightness in refined product markets also continues with low diesel inventories, higher stock drawdowns and the crude futures curve in backwardation. 20 These conditions, along with elevated refined product margins, pose upside risks to domestic fuel prices if geopolitical disruptions persist. Core CPI (CPI excluding Food and Fuel) Core inflation (CPI excluding food and fuel) 21 increased from 3.7 per cent in April to 4.2 per cent in August 2026. Core inflation excluding precious metals 22 registered a sharper increase from 2.2 per cent to 2.9 per cent during the same period ( Table IV.1 ). Precious metals, which are part of the ‘personal care and effects’ sub-group, were a major driver of core inflation over the last year. During April-December 2025, gold and silver prices rose by 41.6 per cent and 66.3 per cent, respectively, accounting for about one-third of the overall core inflation during this period. After peaking in January 2026, precious metal prices have remained range-bound. In terms of sub-components, housing, restaurants and accommodation services, and clothing and footwear were the other major contributors to core inflation ( Chart IV.15 ). IV.3 Decoding the Inflation Dynamics Statistical properties Statistical properties provide useful insights into the nature of the inflation process, in terms of how generalised inflation is, and whether the underlying inflation differs from headline numbers. The distribution of CPI inflation on an average basis during 2026-27 so far (April-August) vis-à-vis 2025-26 indicates a positive skew, reflecting the disproportionately large contribution from precious metals for most months ( Chart IV.17 ). In terms of the monthly trajectory, the increase in inflation during April-August 2026 was accompanied by a widening of inflation divergence across quantiles ( Chart IV.18 ). The widening of inflation divergence across CPI groups is on account of an uptick in inflation in food, pan and tobacco, and personal transport groups. 23 The recent uptick in inflation is also reflected in the CPI headline diffusion indices 24 in August 2026, the weighted distribution of y-o-y headline inflation components shows a shift towards higher inflation categories ( Box IV.1 ). Box IV.1: Measuring Inflation Generalisation through the Diffusion Index When confronted with supply shocks, monetary policy responses are calibrated based on the assessment of second-round effects. If supply shocks are temporary, monetary policy often looks through them, whereas when there are signs of generalisation, policy acts to prevent inflation from becoming embedded in expectations. One critical challenge in this context is to gauge the extent to which inflation has become generalised. This can be assessed by examining whether the initial price pressures remain confined to the directly affected components or have spread to a wider set of items in the CPI basket. A useful measure of this generalisation is the inflation diffusion index, which captures the weighted distribution of item-level price changes in the CPI basket (de Soyres et al., 2026). An increase in the diffusion index in the high inflation categories indicates that price pressures are becoming more widespread across the consumption basket. This can be used along with the headline or core inflation numbers to understand the nature of inflation process. An increase in headline inflation accompanied by a low diffusion index for the high inflation categories is indicative of inflation driven by idiosyncratic supply shocks. On the other hand, surge in diffusion index in the higher inflation category along with the headline inflation number, indicates that inflationary pressures have become more broad-based and generalised. Many countries use diffusion indices alongside other measures of underlying inflation to understand the spread of inflationary pressures. 25 Over the years, the Reserve Bank of India has also examined the distribution of item-level inflation using diffusion indices, inflation distributions and kernel density plots (RBI, Monetary Policy Report, various issues; Nadhanael and Pattanaik, 2010; Hasan et al, 2026). Against this backdrop, the box attempts to compile diffusion indices for inflation in India based on the revised CPI (2024=100) series. The diffusion indices are compiled for i) Headline CPI comprising all items; and ii) Core or CPI excluding food and fuel. 26 The indices are constructed using weighted item-level year-on-year (y-o-y) inflation rates. 27 Conceptually, diffusion indices represent the weighted share of items in the respective CPI basket, categorised into the following four buckets (intervals), aligning it with the inflation target and its tolerance band: i. Below 2 per cent; ii. Between 2 per cent and 4 per cent; iii. Between 4 per cent and 6 per cent; and iv. Above 6 per cent. IV.4 Drivers of Inflation Trajectory This section analyses the evolution of inflation conditions based on the assessment of underlying factors. Imported Inflation The contribution of imported components to domestic inflation picked up in 2026 following the onset of the West Asia conflict. Imported inflation as per the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) (2022-23=100) registered a significant increase up to May 2026, with some pullback thereafter, driven by petroleum products ( Chart IV.20 ). CPI imported inflation also remained elevated during this period, mainly due to higher precious metals prices, given the larger relative weight of precious metals in CPI. 30 The extent of sequential increase in imported inflation in CPI since the onset of the West Asia conflict was lower than that in WPI, partly on account of delayed and partial price increases in petroleum products at the retail level. Cost Conditions Input cost pressures, as measured by WPI industrial raw materials and farm inputs inflation, rose sharply during March-May and remained elevated thereafter. The acceleration in industrial input costs was led by petroleum products, particularly aviation turbine fuel (ATF), high-speed diesel (HSD), naphtha, bitumen, furnace oil, and petroleum coke. The increase in farm input cost inflation was driven mainly by HSD, fertilisers, and nitrogen compounds ( Chart IV.21 ). In the organised corporate sector, staff cost growth (y-o-y) in manufacturing accelerated in Q1:2026-27, following a moderation in Q4:2025-26 driven by strong momentum. In the services sector, y-o-y staff cost growth moderated during both Q4:2025-26 and Q1:2026-27, despite a positive momentum, on account of unfavourable base effects ( Chart IV.22 ). On the outlook for cost and price conditions, infrastructure and services firms expect both input cost and selling price pressures to abate during Q3:2026-27, as per the firms polled in the Reserve Bank’s enterprise surveys. Manufacturing firms expect a moderation in input cost pressures while also expecting an increase in selling prices. Salary outgo pressures are expected to increase for manufacturing firms during Q3:2026-27. In contrast, it is expected to ease for services and infrastructure firms ( Chart IV.23 ). The Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) surveys indicate some sequential moderation in manufacturing firms’ cost pressures after the sharp increase following the onset of the West Asia conflict. Input price pressures reported by manufacturing firms eased gradually up to August 2026 after peaking in April. Output price pressures followed a broadly similar trajectory. Both input and output prices inched up in September. The manufacturing PMI input-output price gap turned positive in March 2026, indicating weak pass-through of input costs to selling prices. Although the gap narrowed from its March peak, it remained positive in August, suggesting some pent-up pass-through ( Chart IV.24a ). In the services sector, operating cost pressures eased gradually up to July before a mild pick-up in August 2026. Selling price pressures also moderated up to June but increased in July-August. Consequently, the services PMI input-output price gap narrowed significantly in August ( Chart IV.24b ). Similar trends were observed for Output and Input Producer Price Index (PPI) 31 for manufactured products during April-August 2026. For most industry groups, pace of increase in input prices was faster than that of output prices, suggesting that the full extent of input price rise may not have been passed on to output prices ( Chart IV.25 ). At the aggregate level, however, output prices rose faster than input prices driven by coke and refined petroleum products. Margins Food price margins 32 have recorded a mixed trend in the recent period. Retail margins for cereals remained stable during April-September 2026. Margins for pulses remained stable until June before moderating during July-September. For TOP vegetables, margins picked up since April. In case of edible oils, margins peaked in May 2026 but remained range-bound thereafter ( Chart IV.26 ). In terms of the relative contribution of supply and demand factors in conditioning inflation dynamics, the evidence points towards the dissipation of both favourable supply and benign demand conditions, which led to increase in inflation in 2026-27 so far ( Box IV.2 ). Box IV.2: What Drives Inflation in India? Disentangling Demand and Supply Factors Disentangling the relative roles of demand and supply factors in driving inflation is critical for an inflation-targeting central bank to calibrate appropriate policy response. Demand-driven inflation typically calls for monetary tightening, while supply-driven inflation creates difficult policy trade-offs as it is often accompanied by a slowdown in growth. In case of India, the recent experience of inflation significantly undershooting the target before a sharp reversal merits a thorough examination of the role of demand and supply factors in shaping the inflation dynamics. Empirical literature has adopted different approaches to disentangle the contributions of aggregate demand and supply conditions such as identifying the cyclical component of inflation by examining its relationship with economic activity as proposed by Stock and Watson (2020). Another approach is to explicitly decompose inflation into demand and supply-driven components using price and quantity information at the commodity or consumption-category level (Shapiro, 2024 33 and Shekhar, Kishore and Bhoi, 2023). More recently, Eickmeier and Hofmann (2025) have developed a structural factor model to identify aggregate demand and supply conditions using a broad set of inflation and real activity indicators. Their methodology exploits the common variation across a large number of macroeconomic series and identifies demand and supply factors through theoretically motivated sign restrictions on factor loadings. The demand factor is characterised by positive co-movement between inflation and economic activity, whereas the supply factor is associated with opposite movements in inflation and economic activity. This framework enables the construction of aggregate indicators of demand and supply conditions and facilitates an assessment of their contribution to inflation dynamics over time. This factor-based approach is applied to the Indian economy to identify indicators of aggregate demand and supply conditions and examine their role in the evolution of inflation in India. Compared with approaches that focus primarily on cyclical inflation or commodity-level price and quantity responses, the proposed framework incorporates information from a broader set of macroeconomic variables. Data The dataset includes a broad set of inflation measures including headline CPI, house price index, and other group/sub-group-wise inflation. The real-activity block includes GDP and expenditure components, gross and sectoral GVA indices, and other demand proxies such as diesel consumption and capacity utilisation. Other global price indicators like gold, copper, Brent crude oil and fertiliser prices are also included. 34 Methodology The empirical strategy uses a factor model estimated by employing principal component analysis on quarterly macroeconomic time series data for India. Factor identification follows the standard supply-demand analysis based on randomly generated orthogonal rotations. The demand factor is identified as one that loads positively on inflation measures and real-activity measures. The supply factor is identified as one that loads negatively on inflation measures and positively on real-activity measures. Sign restrictions are imposed across key variables while allowing some variables to remain unrestricted. Once the demand and supply factors are identified 35 , Fry-Pagan median target approach is used to select accepted rotation closest to the median target. Results The findings indicate that the recent episode of inflation declining from H2:2024-25 to H2:2025-26 was driven by a weakening of demand as well as easy supply conditions ( Chart IV.2.1 and Chart IV.2.2 ). Latest data for Q1:2026-27 show closing of negative demand conditions as well as waning of easy supply conditions. Demand factor converged to almost zero levels during Q1 as economic activity strengthened despite global shocks and emerging supply side pressures. As growth has surprised on the upside and inflation is showing early signs of generalisation, this indicates waning of favourable factors that kept inflation benign during 2025-26 and potential pressures going forward. IV.5 Conclusion Headline inflation has increased steadily throughout 2026-27 (up to August), initially driven by higher food and fuel inflation but showing signs of broad-based price pressures in recent months. The impact of El Niño conditions and deficient southwest monsoon is increasingly reflected in food prices. Core inflation recorded a pick-up along with incipient signs of generalisation. Going forward, there is a material risk that supply-side pressures in food may remain unabated as weather uncertainties persist and global oil prices continue to remain volatile. In this context, generalisation of inflation through second-round effects remains a major risk from the firming up of demand conditions, given strong growth impulses.
