BANCO DE ESPAÑA 9 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 1 Introduction Cash design is not only a matter of visual aesthetics and security features, but also of how people implicitly perceive, interpret, and emotionally respond to cash during daily interactions. In this context, voice analysis offers a promising bridge between cash perception research and psychophysiological measurement, as vocal signals can reflect subtle changes in emotional arousal, cognitive load, confidence, and perceived security. Understanding these implicit human reactions is fundamental in cash design to optimize currency usability and the effectiveness of anti-counterfeiting measures. The aim of this review is to offer a broad and connected perspective on voice analysis, encompassing the physiological bases of vocal production, its relationship with emotional expression, and the technological tools currently available for extracting acoustic features in perception and affective-computing research. In doing so, the work synthesizes the present state of Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) technologies while preserving a conceptual and accessible perspective grounded in psychology. Rather than offering an exhaustive technical review of every computational component, the goal is to present a coherent, interdisciplinary overview that bridges psychophysiology, acoustics, and machine-learning approaches to emotional voice analysis. SER is situated within the broader domain of Automatic Emotion Recognition (AER), a field that integrates multiple biosignals, such as EEG (electroencephalography), facial expressions, gestures, or speech, to infer affective states. Within this ecosystem, the human voice stands out as a unique psychophysiological signal: it arises from the coordination of breathing, vocal-fold movement, and articulation, all of which change with emotional, cognitive, and autonomic states (De Lope & Graña, 2023). Understanding these biological mechanisms is therefore essential for interpreting how emotions shape the acoustic signal. For this reason, the document begins by outlining the physiological and anatomical bases of vocal production, following authors who argue that acoustic analyses must be

grounded in vocal biomechanics. Building on this theoretical foundation, the second section examines how emotional states influence key acoustic features such as fundamental frequency, intensity, spectral balance, and temporal dynamics. Recent reviews show that emotions reliably shape vocal acoustics, allowing speech to convey meaningful psychophysiological information (Van Puyvelde et al., 2018; Schewski et al., 2025). These relationships are central both to psychological research and to the development of computational models that aim to decode emotions from speech. The study then presents the complete Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) methodological pipeline, outlining the process of transforming raw audio into emotional labels. These stages include audio-source selection, preprocessing, acoustic feature extraction, and classification using either classical machine-learning algorithms or modern deep-learning architectures. Finally, after describing the pipeline, the document provides a structured overview of the most relevant technological tools for implementing SER, ranging from commercial to open-source options. This includes commercial approaches (e.g., audEERING, iMotions), pretrained model pipelines with external or internal classifiers, custom SER systems built from scratch, and modular multimodal frameworks such as the MixedEmotions Toolbox. By comparing these alternatives, practical considerations that researchers must evaluate when selecting tools for academic or applied contexts are highlighted, including model interpretability, data requirements, and computational costs.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 10 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 Although this review focuses on the human voice as a neurophysiological marker for implicit emotion, it is motivated by the broader research context of neurodesign for cash. Within the Neurocash ® framework, the Innovation & Development unit of the Banco de España aims to establish an objective, multidimensional methodology to evaluate the public’s perception of banknotes. By integrating neuroscientific tools and implicit behavioral measures, this project seeks to overcome the traditional limitations of subjective surveys, capturing the subconscious emotional and cognitive reactions of users when interacting with currency (Banco de España, n.d.; Ortuño et al., 2020). Specifically applied to cash perception research, the Neurocash ® methodology provides cash designers with a robust, quantitative tool to optimize the design process. By capturing these acoustic fluctuations during exposure to or evaluation of currency features, the human voice can complement other biometric and behavioral measures within this framework. This allows for the precise evaluation of how different visual and tactile elements capture attention, how cognitive workload is modulated during the verification of security features, and how these factors influence the user’s implicit trust and perceived security (Banco de España, n.d.; Ortuño et al., 2020). By systematically analyzing these biometric, neurophysiological, and vocal responses, Neurocash ® acts as a scientific bridge that enhances the aesthetics, intuitive usability, and anti-counterfeiting resilience of banknotes throughout their entire lifecycle. 1.1 Justification of the review Despite the rapid growth of Speech Emotion Recognition (SER), existing reviews remain fragmented and often focus on only one part of the field. Most surveys highlight technical advances, especially, new machine-learning models and self-supervised speech methods, while giving much less attention to the psychophysiological and acoustic principles that support emotional expression in the voice. As a result, many overviews adopt a mainly computational viewpoint, with

limited connection to the biological mechanisms of vocal production or to the well-established acoustic markers of emotion. This limitation in the review literature reflects a broader problem in the field: a lack of integration across disciplines. Psychophysiology, vocal acoustics, and deep-learning-based SER systems are often treated as separate research areas, even though they naturally depend on one another. Because of this separation, key concepts, such as subglottal pressure changes, vocal-fold behaviour, prosodic shifts, and spectral patterns, rarely appear together in computational surveys. This reduces the interpretability of SER models and makes it harder to understand the psychophysiological meaning of the features these systems extract. A further challenge is that research on how emotions influence vocal acoustics is spread across different fields such as clinical voice science, neuroscience, phonetics, and machine learning. Because these findings are rarely brought together, it is difficult to build a clear, unified understanding of how emotional processes shape the voice and how these cues are used in SER systems. For these reasons, an integrative review that unifies physiological mechanisms, acoustic correlates, psychological theory, and contemporary SER methodologies is necessary. The present work aims to consolidate these domains into a coherent conceptual framework, offering the scientific community a comprehensive, interdisciplinary account of how emotions are encoded and decoded through the human voice.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 11 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 2 Methods This article was written as a narrative integrative review, a method that brings together different types of evidence from fields such as psychophysiology, acoustics, speech science, affective computing, and machine learning. This type of review makes it possible to combine empirical studies, theoretical work, technical documentation, and methodological papers to create a broad understanding of a research area. Because Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) involves many disciplines, this approach is well suited to summarizing its physiological, acoustic, and computational aspects within a single framework. 2.1 Search Strategy and Sources Between October 2025 and February 2026, a broad literature search was performed across the following databases and platforms: • Google Scholar • PubMed (physiology, voice science) • IEEE Xplore (machine learning, signal processing) • ACM Digital Library [Human Computer Interaction (HCI), affective computing] • arXiv (deep learning and transformer-based SER studies) • Publisher websites for technical documentation (e.g., audEERING, iMotions, Affectiva, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services) • GitHub repositories for open-source SER toolkits. The search combined keywords and Boolean operators such as: “speech emotion recognition” OR “SER” OR “emotional prosody” OR “acoustic correlates of emotion” OR “self-supervised speech models” OR “wav2vec2” OR “HuBERT” OR “WavLM” OR “affective computing” OR “voice physiology” OR “emotion acoustics”. 2.2 Inclusion Criteria Sources were included if they met at least one of the following criteria: • Conceptual relevance to the physiological, psychological, or computational foundations of emotional voice production (e.g., Liebenthal et al., 2016). • Empirical or methodological contribution to acoustic correlates of emotion, vocal stress, or prosody (e.g., Van Puyvelde et al., 2018; Schewski et al., 2025).

Thematic clustering into core domains: — Vocal physiology and how the voice is produced (breathing, vocal folds, and articulation). — How emotions shape the acoustic signal (changes in pitch/F0, loudness, voice quality, and timing). — The SER pipeline (audio collection, preprocessing, feature extraction, and classification methods). — Emotional speech datasets used for training and evaluation (e.g., EmoDB, RAVDESS, IEMOCAP). — Types of acoustic features (prosodic, spectral, cepstral, energy related, temporal/fluency features, and standard sets like eGeMAPS).

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 14 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 3 Definition and Applications of SER 3.1 Definition Within the broader field of Automatic Emotion Recognition (AER), which includes analyses based on EEG, gestures, facial expressions, and other biometric signals, we find Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), whose primary function is to convert audio into text. This process relies on signal processing and machine learning methods that are shared with emotion related systems (De Lope & Graña, 2023). One of ASR’s key subfields is Speech Emotion Recognition (SER), which uses similar signal processing tools such as speech rate, pitch, and prosody to identify and classify emotions present in speech. Recent work highlights the importance of these acoustic cues in predicting emotional states accurately (Van Puyvelde et al., 2018; Schewski et al., 2025). 3.2 Applications SER is used in many areas, including psychology, healthcare, and marketing. However, for the purposes of this work, in the context of implicit perception measurement, we focus on its role within the Internet of Things (IoT). In IoT environments, devices interact continuously with users, and emotional information can help these systems adjust their behaviour, personalise their responses, and create more natural interactions (Chang et al., 2024). The IoT ecosystem includes several interaction focused fields, such as Human–Computer Interaction (HCI), Human– Machine Interaction (HMI), Human–Robot Interaction (HRI), and Affective Computing. Within this ecosystem, SER becomes especially relevant for Affective Computing, a field whose goal is to detect and interpret human emotions so that systems can adapt affectively. This “affective layer” is what distinguishes Affective Computing from other interaction oriented disciplines: • HCI, HMI, and HRI focus on the mechanics and design of interaction, such as interfaces, usability, ergonomics, and task performance, without necessarily analysing emotional states. • Affective Computing, in contrast, explicitly incorporates emotion. It studies how machines can understand
and respond to the user’s affective signals (Wang et al., 2022), making SER a key component for enabling emotionally adaptive behaviour.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 15 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 4 Voice Physiology and Acoustic Correlates of Emotion As illustrated in Figure 1, voice production begins with airflow originating in the lungs. The vocal folds, two bands of tissue located in the larynx between the base of the tongue and the top of the trachea, remain open during breathing and close during phonation (National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders [NIDCD, n.d.]). When speaking, the diaphragm contracts to expand the thoracic cavity, allowing the lungs to fill with air before releasing it during exhalation, which initiates the phonatory process (Ladefoged, 2001). Sound is produced when exhaled air passes through the closed vocal folds, increasing subglottal pressure until they separate, allowing air to flow through the glottis. The glottis widens during breathing and narrows during voice production (NIDCD, n.d.; Zhang, 2016). Rapid airflow creates pressure changes that bring the vocal folds back together, causing them to vibrate and generate sound. Typical speech requires normal vibratory behaviour of both the larynx and the vocal folds (Morrison, Rammage, Nichol, Pullan, & May, 1994). Once phonation is understood, further components of speech production can be defined, namely articulation and resonance. Vocal production relies on the coordinated action of several subsystems: • The respiratory phase: during which air exits the lungs (Morrison, Rammage, Nichol, Pullan, & May, 1994). BANCO DE ESPAÑA 16 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 • Phonation: in which airflow sets the vocal folds into vibration (Morrison, Rammage, Nichol, Pullan, & May, 1994). • Articulation, involving lips, tongue, teeth, and hard palate. • Resonance, produced by the oral and nasal cavities that amplify and shape the voice (NIDCD, n.d.). Physiological factors such as pitch, influenced by vocal ‑fold length and tension; intensity, determined by airflow force and vibratory amplitude; timbre, shaped by the vocal tract’s configuration; and duration, defined by the length of vocal‑fold vibration, all contribute to the acoustic characteristics of the human voice (Morrison, Rammage, Nichol, Pullan, & May, 1994 & Zhang, 2016).

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 17 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 5 Emotions and their Influence on Acoustics Emotions influence the way our voice sounds because they affect how we breathe, how the larynx is positioned, and how the vocal tract moves. In psychology, emotions are understood as complex reactions that include thoughts, bodily changes, and expressive behaviours, all of which can shape our vocal output (American Psychological Association [APA], n.d.). Research shows that emotional states modify key acoustic features, such as fundamental frequency (F0), loudness, spectral balance or voice quality, and timing, through physiological changes in subglottal pressure, vocal fold vibration, and the configuration of the vocal tract (Liebenthal et al., 2016; Van Puyvelde et al., 2018). For example, positive emotions often occur alongside facial and postural changes like smiling, which alter the shape of the vocal tract and tend to produce a higher, brighter ‑sounding voice. More generally, high ‑arousal emotions such as joy or anger are associated with louder voices and greater variation in intensity than low ‑arousal states like sadness or tenderness (Liebenthal et al., 2016). Emotional and cognitive demands also influence vocal behaviour. When people are under cognitive– emotional load, their voices show measurable shifts in F0, loudness, and perturbation ‑based voice measures, reflecting the combined effect of attention, mental effort, and affective state on vocal production (Van Mersbergen & Payne, 2021; Van Puyvelde et al., 2018). Clinical reviews further show that increased tension in the larynx can produce rougher voice quality and reduced vocal power, illustrating how physiological stress and emotional strain affect the sound of the voice (Eastwood et al., 2015). Taken together, these findings support the idea that emotions influence speech through coordinated changes in bodily, cognitive, and expressive systems, consistent with the three‑component model of emotion. A growing body of research demonstrates that emotions

also shape prosody, patterns of pitch, rhythm, and intonation, in reliable ways. A large review of speech produced under negative emotions, stress, and cognitive load shows that anger, fear, anxiety, and stress frequently involve increases in F0 and, in some cases, noticeable changes in speech rate or pausing, although results vary across studies (Schewski et al., 2025). Evidence from acted emotional speech in Mexican Spanish similarly reveals distinct prosodic profiles: emocionado [excited] and enojado [angry] show high F0 values, wide pitch movements, and rising bitonal accents, while tranquilo [calm] and triste [sad] display flatter, more even pitch contours with smaller differences between syllables. Neutral utterances follow the expected declarative pattern typical of Central Mexican Spanish (González Franco et al., 2023).

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 18 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 6 Methodological Pipeline SER Once we understand how the voice is produced and how emotions can shape it, we can look at how Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) systems go from a simple audio recording to identifying the emotion behind it. This process typically involves four stages: • Audio source selection: Studies may employ spontaneous speech recordings or standardized emotional speech databases. Widely used corpora, such as EmoDB (Burkhardt et al., 2005), RAVDESS (Livingstone & Russo, 2018), and IEMOCAP (Busso et al., 2008), provide controlled, annotated emotional material essential for SER benchmarking. • Data preprocessing: Includes denoising, normalization, segmentation, and amplitude or sampling ‑rate standardization to ensure signal quality and consistency across recordings (De Lope & Graña, 2023). • Feature extraction: Extracted acoustic features typically involve pitch, prosodic dynamics, spectral energy, speech rate, and voice quality. In many studies, researchers rely on standardized sets like eGeMAPS or openSMILE so that acoustic features remain comparable across different projects (Eyben et al., 2016). • Classification approaches: SER tasks may be addressed using traditional machine ‑learning models (e.g., SVMs, Random Forests) as well as deep learning architectures (e.g., CNN ‑, RNN ‑, or transformer ‑based systems) trained on emotional speech databases (De Lope & Graña, 2023). 6.1 Emotional Speech Databases Table 1 presents a comparison of emotional speech databases according to the number of target emotions, language, availability of visual and acoustic modalities, whether speech is acted or natural, speaker demographics, and total number of utterances (De Lope & Graña, 2023). These databases can be used both to train deep learning models for emotion recognition and to benchmark different SER approaches.

Together, these studies demonstrate that preprocessing is not an optional step but a critical requirement for ensuring reliability, reproducibility, and model robustness in SER research. 6.3 Feature extraction A speech recording contains thousands of measurable acoustic properties, many of which are useful for Speech Emotion Recognition (SER). Recent reviews group these properties into several main categories, temporal, prosodic, spectral, cepstral, and energy‑related features, and describe standardized feature sets developed for paralinguistic analysis (De Lope & Graña, 2023; Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023). 6.3.1 Temporal and fluency features Temporal features describe how speech unfolds over time. They include overall duration, speech rate, syllable timing, rhythm, and the presence or length of pauses, as well as distinctions between vocalic and non ‑vocalic segments. These patterns often change with emotional arousal or cognitive load and are frequently included in both traditional feature sets and deep‑learning SER models (Byun & Lee, 2021; De Lope & Graña, 2023). 6.3.2 Prosodic features Prosodic features relate to pitch and loudness patterns, such as fundamental frequency (F0), intonation contours, intensity, accentuation, and overall variability. Because they reflect adjustments in phonation and respiration, prosodic cues are reliably associated with emotional expression in speech (Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023; De Lope & Graña, 2023). 6.3.3 Spectral features Spectral features capture how energy is distributed across frequencies. They include formants, spectral centroid, roll‑off, kurtosis, and various energy bands, as well as spectrogram‑based representations such as Mel‑spectrograms. These features reflect vocal ‑tract configuration and are essential in both classical machine ‑learning and deep learning–based SER systems (Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023). 6.3.4 Cepstral features Widely used in speech and emotion recognition, cepstral coefficients such as MFCCs, delta and delta

‑delta coefficients, GFCCs, and LPCCs capture perceptually and physiologically meaningful aspects of the signal. Many SER studies adopt them as core inputs for both machine ‑learning and neural architectures (Byun & Lee, 2021; Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023). 6.3.5 Energy‑based features Energy features measure the overall power of the signal and its variation over time. Metrics such as root mean square (RMS) energy can help differentiate high ‑arousal from low‑arousal emotional states (Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023).

They remain useful complementary indicators in multi ‑feature SER models (Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023). 6.3.7 Predefined standardized feature sets Standard feature sets like eGeMAPS, GeMAPS, and ComParE (available in the openSMIL E toolkit) combine many of the audio features mentioned earlier into well ‑tested, ready‑to‑use configurations. These sets are widely used in affective computing and other speech‑related research areas (audEERING, n.d.; De Lope & Graña, 2023). Finally, current SER resea rch often compares these handcrafted features with representations learned directly from data, such as embeddings derived from self ‑supervised learning (SSL) models or automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. Even so, traditional feature categories remain essential for benchmarking and interpreting these newer approaches (Gao et al., 2024). BANCO DE ESPAÑA 22 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 6.4 Classifier Approaches: Conventional (Classical Machine Learning) vs. Deep Learning Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) systems are commonly divided into two major methodological families. The first relies on conventional machine ‑learning models built on hand ‑crafted acoustic features, while the second uses deep learning techniques that learn informative representations directly from the speech signal or from its time–frequency transformations. This section provides an overview of the modelling assumptions, typical input features, representative algorithms, and the main advantages and limitations associated with each approach. A comprehensive survey of the field discusses these developments in detail and motivates the comparison presented here (Kaur & Singh, 2023). 6.4.1 Conventional methods (classical machine learning) • Modelling pipeline: Conventional Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) methods begin by extracting a set of hand-crafted features from the audio signal. These features describe core aspects of the voice, such as pitch, loudness, rhythmic patterns, and widely used acoustic descriptors like Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs), which summarise how energy is distributed across frequency bands. After these features are obtained, they are passed to a traditional machine-learning classifier, such as Support Vector Machines, k-Nearest Neighbours, Naïve Bayes, decision trees or Random Forests, Gaussian Mixture Models, or Hidden Markov Models, which learns to distinguish between emotional categories. Because these features are manually designed rather than learned automatically, this approach tends to work reliably even when only limited training data are available. It is also generally considered more transparent and easier to interpret than modern deep-learning systems. MFCCs, in particular, have a long history in speech processing research, originating in the influential work of Davis and Mermelstein (1980). • Representative classifiers: — Support Vector Machines (SVMs): SVMs try to find the best boundary that separates different emotion classes in the feature space, keeping the classes as

far apart as possible. They were widely used in early SER systems (Kaur & Singh, 2023). — k-Nearest Neighbours (k-NN): k-NN classifies a new speech sample by checking which labelled samples it most closely resembles and assigning it the majority emotion among those neighbours (Kaur & Singh, 2023). — Naïve Bayes: A simple probabilistic model that estimates which emotion is most likely based on the features, assuming each feature contributes independently (Kaur & Singh, 2023). — Decision Trees / Random Forests: hierarchical partitioning; Decision trees split the data step by step based on feature values until they reach an emotion label. Random Forests combine many such trees, which makes them more stable and often more accurate, for example, outperforming SVMs on some SER datasets (Yan et al., 2020). — Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs): GMMs represent each emotion as a combination of several Gaussian (bell-shaped) distributions. The model then estimates which emotion’s distribution best fits the input speech (Bishop, 2006).

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 23 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 — Hidden Markov Models (HMMs): HMMs model speech as a sequence of short frames and capture how acoustic patterns change over time. They are especially useful for time-dependent signals like speech (Rabiner,1989). • Strengths and limitations: Conventional pipelines are computationally light, perform reasonably well with small, labelled datasets, and facilitate diagnostics (e.g., feature importance). However, performance strongly depends on the quality of the hand-crafted features, and classical models may face challenges when conditions change (e.g., speaker variation, noise, or language differences); limited multimodal fusion support is another constraint (Lian et al., 2023, Entropy). 6.4.2 Deep learning methods • Modelling pipeline: Deep learning models tend to discover acoustic patterns on their own, whether they work directly with the waveform or with spectral representations. In doing so, they reduce the need for manually engineered features and instead discover informative representations automatically. A variety of neural encoder architectures are commonly used for this purpose. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are effective for analysing the two-dimensional structure of spectrograms, capturing local spectro-temporal patterns. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), including LSTMs and GRUs, are suited to modelling how emotional cues evolve over time in the speech signal. Many SER systems combine these strengths through hybrid CNN–RNN models, which first extract local acoustic patterns and then learn their temporal dependencies. More recently, Transformer-based encoders have become prominent, using multi-head self-attention to capture long-range relationships across the speech sequence (Latif et al., 2023). • Representative deep learning model families: — Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs): CNNs extract local patterns from spectrograms (e.g., pitch, formants, energy) and are very effective when SER is formulated as an image-like problem. They were among the first deep models to outperform classical MFCC+SVM pipelines (Neumann & Vu, 2017; Satt et al., 2017). — Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs):

RNNs, especially LSTMs and GRUs, model the temporal dynamics of speech, capturing how emotions evolve across frames. They became a standard baseline for sequence modelling in SER before Transformers gained traction (Trigeorgis et al., 2016; Satt et al., 2017). — CNN–RNN hybrids: Hybrid models combine CNNs for spectral feature extraction with RNNs for temporal modelling. This architecture is common in SER because it combines the strengths of both approaches: they capture local spectrotemporal details while also modelling how the signal evolves over time (Trigeorgis et al., 2016; Abdelhamid et al., 2022). — Variational Autoencoders (VAEs): learn compressed emotional representations without labels. They are used for feature learning, noise reduction, or generating synthetic emotional speech (Latif et al., 2018).

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 24 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 — Transformer-based models: Transformers use self-attention to model long-range dependencies and have become the most powerful architecture in SER. Pretrained variants like wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT dominate current benchmarks (Pepino et al., 2021; Latif et al., 2023). — Supervised vs. Self-supervised learning: • Supervised learning requires labelled emotional audio and was the traditional setup for CNN/RNN models. Its performance depends strongly on dataset size and annotation quality (Trigeorgis et al., 2016). • Self-supervised learning (SSL) learns general speech features from unlabelled audio (e.g., wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT), achieving far better generalisation in low-resource emotional datasets (Hsu et al., 2021; Pepino et al., 2021). • Novelties: — Pretrained models: One of the biggest recent advances is the use of models like wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT. They are first trained on huge amounts of unlabelled audio and then fine-tuned for emotion recognition. This helps a lot when emotional datasets are small and currently give some of the strongest results, especially for valence (Pepino et al., 2021; Hsu et al., 2021; Wagner et al., 2023). — Multimodal models: Deep learning also makes it easy to combine multiple signals at once, for example, speech together with facial expressions or text. Different “fusion” strategies (early, late or intermediate) are used to mix these modalities, and recent surveys summarise the main techniques and datasets in multimodal emotion recognition (Lian et al., 2023). — Data augmentation: Since emotional datasets are often small, data augmentation is increasingly used to improve model robustness. Typical techniques include pitch shifting, time-stretching, adding noise, SpecAugment, vocal tract length perturbation and synthetic data generation. These methods improve generalisation, especially for deep models working in low-resource conditions (Ko et al., 2015; Park et al., 2019; Atmaja & Sasou, 2022; Chatziagapi et al., 2019; Qu et al., 2022).

• Strengths and limitations. Deep learning eliminates manual feature design, learns non ‑linear hierarchical patterns, scales with data, and integrates multimodal cues. However, these advantages come with trade‑offs: deep models usually require large amounts of labelled data (although this can be reduced through self‑supervised or transfer learning), they are harder to interpret, and they demand more computational resources during training and deployment (Latif et al., 2023; Wagner et al., 2023). The main differences between conventional and deep learning approaches are summarized in Figure 4, including their respective architectures, advantages, and limitations.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 25 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 6.4.3 Is there an optimal model? A recurrent theme in the literature is that there is no single optimal model for Speech Emotion Recognition (SER). As highlighted by De Lope and Graña (2023), SER encompasses a wide spectrum of classical machine learning methods and deep learning architectures, each with different strengths depending on the characteristics of the data and the task at hand. Their review shows that performance varies substantially across datasets, languages, emotional taxonomies, and feature extraction strategies, and that both classical and deep learning approaches continue to coexist in SER research. This diversity of methods reflects that model choice is inherently problemdependent rather than universal. In practical terms, this means that the “best” model depends on what the researcher seeks to achieve, for example, maximising accuracy, ensuring interpretability, working with limited training data, or integrating multimodal inputs. As De Lope and Graña (2023) emphasise, SER systems are highly sensitive to dataset properties and experimental conditions, and no approach consistently outperforms all others across benchmarks. Thus, the field does not converge toward a single optimal classifier, but rather toward a set of techniques that must be matched to the specific requirements of each application. BANCO DE ESPAÑA 26 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 7 Complementary Approach to SER A complementary approach to Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) is Natural Language Processing (NLP), which focuses on analysing the verbal content of speech rather than its acoustic properties. NLP requires converting the audio signal into text using an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) system. Modern ASR pipelines, covered extensively in standard NLP textbooks, transform the speech waveform into linguistic units that can be processed computationally (Jurafsky & Martin, 2026). Once the speech is transcribed, NLP techniques can be applied to perform lexical, syntactic, and semantic analyses of the text. One widely used NLP application is Sentiment Analysis, which identifies explicit or implicit emotional content expressed through words, considering both word frequency and contextual meaning. Sentiment analysis is recognised as a core task within NLP , enabling the detection of attitudes, affect, and evaluative language in written or transcribed text (Ramdani, 2025; Jurafsky & Martin, 2026).

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 30 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 8.4 Create a model from scratch Developing a custom SER system involves manually designing and integrating each component of the pipeline. This approach offers full control over how audio is processed, which features are extracted, and how the classifier is built, but it also introduces greater technical complexity. • The workflow typically follows the previously reviewed five stages: 1. Audio acquisition: The process begins with selecting an audio source, either from existing emotional speech datasets such as EmoDB (Burkhardt et al., 2005), RAVDESS (Livingstone and Russo, 2018), or IEMOCAP (Busso et al., 2008), or from self ‑recorded material. 2. Preprocessing: Before analysis, the audio must be cleaned and normalized to ensure consistent signal quality. Standard preprocessing steps include noise reduction, segmentation, silence trimming, and amplitude or sampling ‑rate normalization (De Lope & Graña, 2023; Katti & Sumana, 2023). These operations are essential because inadequate preprocessing negatively affects feature extraction and classifier performance. 3. Feature extraction: Once the signal is prepared, relevant acoustic properties are extracted. Emotional information is typically encoded in temporal, prosodic, spectral, and cepstral features, such as pitch, duration, energy, MFCCs, and formants—commonly used in traditional SER systems (De Lope & Graña, 2023; Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023; Byun & Lee, 2021). 4. Classifier design: After feature extraction, a classifier is trained to map the acoustic descriptors to emotional categories. Conventional machine ‑learning methods include SVMs, k ‑NN, and Random Forests (Kaur & Singh, 2023; Yan et al., 2020), whereas deep‑learning approaches such as CNNs, RNNs, and hybrid CNN‑RNN architectures have become increasingly common for modelling both spectral and temporal patterns (Latif et al., 2023; Trigeorgis et al., 2016; Pepino et al., 2021). 5. Emotion prediction: Finally, the system outputs emotion labels or dimensional affect scores based on the trained model.

The platform was developed through a collaboration between several European institutions, including the National University of Ireland, Galway (Ireland), the University of Passau (Germany), the Universidad Politécnica de Madrid (Spain), and the Brno University of Technology (Czech Republic). The MixedEmotions Toolbox provides a unified framework that enables automatic extraction of emotions across modalities and supports lexical and semantic analysis. For Speech Emotion Recognition (SER), the toolbox includes the “Emotion Recognition Audio (m6)” module, which implements a complete SER pipeline—from acoustic feature extraction to modelbased emotion prediction—returning continuous affect estimates such as arousal and valence (Buitelaar et al., 2018). The platform can be downloaded from GitHub and executed using Docker containers, as each module is packaged as an independent microservice that can be deployed without dependency issues (Buitelaar et al., 2018).

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 32 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 9 Discussion 9.1 Overview and Interpretation of the Synthesis This review integrates evidence from psychophysiology, vocal acoustics, and contemporary Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) to clarify how emotional information is encoded and decoded through the human voice. Vocal expression arises from coordinated respiratory, laryngeal, and articulatory mechanisms that systematically shape acoustic features such as pitch, intensity, spectral balance, and temporal dynamics. From this perspective, SER is not only a classification task, but a modelling process grounded in how the vocal system functions physiologically and how these mechanisms give rise to measurable acoustic markers of affect. 9.2 Interdisciplinary Integration and Added Value A major contribution of this review is the integration of domains that are often treated separately. By linking physiological mechanisms with acoustic correlates, psychological interpretation, and machinelearning methodologies, the review shows how internal states are translated into features that SER systems can analyse. This interdisciplinary perspective improves interpretability, supports more informed feature selection, and provides a stronger foundation for applications in HCI, HRI, and IoT, where systems must adapt to users’ emotional states. 9.3 Methodological Heterogeneity in SER The field exhibits substantial heterogeneity at multiple levels: • Data: emotional classifications, acted versus naturalistic speech, language coverage, recording conditions, and speaker diversity vary widely across databases; these factors directly affect benchmark comparability and model generalizability. • Features and representations: The field ranges from using handcrafted features like prosody and MFCCs to relying on deep ‑learned and self ‑supervised representations, and this choice affects both model performance and the interpretability of the results. • Modelling approaches: Classical machine ‑learning models still work well when data are limited and are easier to interpret, while deep learning, especially self ‑supervised models, delivers stronger performance and better transfer, but at the cost of more computation and lower

interpretability. Given these sources of variation, there is no single optimal model for SER. Instead, model choice should be matched to the task, data regime, constraints on interpretability, and deployment context. 9.4 Implications for Research and Practice Connecting computational methods to what we know about how the voice works offers two clear benefits: First, it helps researchers make better decisions when choosing acoustic features and analysing errors. If a model misclassifies an emotion, the mistake can often be linked to specific physiological or articulatory factors—such as changes in vocalfold vibration or airflow—rather than being treated as an unexplained blackbox outcome.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 33 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 Second, incorporating knowledge about vocal behaviour into the model design allows developers to include constraints that reflect how real speech is produced. These constraints, whether introduced through architecture or the training process, make the system more robust when dealing with background noise, different speakers, or natural variation in emotional expression. In applied fields such as HCI, HRI, and IoT, this approach leads to systems that react more appropriately to users’ emotions while remaining interpretable for developers and practitioners. In studies related to cash perception, these methods can help analyse emotional and cognitive reactions to cash design and perceptions of security. This aligns with the goals of the Neurocash ® framework, which focuses on understanding emotional impact, cognitive processing, visual impact, and the public’s sense of safety when interacting with cash (Banco de España, n.d.; Ortuño et al., 2020). 9.5 Potential Application to Cash Perception Research Situated within the Neurocash ® methodology, SER can act as an additional, noninvasive bio-signal to complement gaze, tactility and other physiological measures when evaluating cash prototypes, both in laboratory and virtual neurodesign settings. By capturing vocal features associated with arousal, valence and cognitive load during taskoriented interactions with cash stimuli, SER could help predict acceptance, clarity and perceived security of design elements. Moreover, integrating SER with current Neurocash ® multimodal studies, such as EEG, gesture analysis and other biometric indicators, would provide a more holistic and robust view of implicit perception, enriching the project’s ability to identify how users emotionally and cognitively experience cashrelated designs. 9.6 Limitations of the Present Review This work is a narrative integrative review rather than a systematic review or meta ‑analysis. As such, the goal was conceptual synthesis across heterogeneous literatures rather than quantitative aggregation. Because the sources span more than four

decades of research (approximately 1980–2026), methodological conventions and technological capabilities vary considerably, which may limit direct comparability across studies. Although the search spanned multiple scholarly databases, preprint servers, and technical documentation, coverage cannot be exhaustive. In addition, the rapid pace of advances in deep learning and self ‑supervised speech modelling implies that specific tools and benchmarks may evolve quickly. Finally, while this review emphasizes physiological grounding and interdisciplinary integration, it does not resolve ongoing challenges in cross ‑lingual generalization, naturalistic emotion capture, and fine‑grained affect modelling (e.g., mixed emotions, appraisal dimensions, context dependence). 9.7 Future Directions Building on the perspective developed in this review, several areas deserve attention: • More natural and cross‑language data. • Create larger and more diverse emotion‑speech datasets that: — Use clear and consistent ways of labelling emotions.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 34 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 — Include detailed information about speakers and situations. — Capture emotions in real, everyday scenarios, not only acted speech. This would help systems work better across different people, contexts, and languages. • Models guided by how the voice works physically: Design models that consider what we know about voice production, for example, how pitch changes, how air pressure works, or how the tongue and lips move when emotions shift. Combining these understandable features with modern deep ‑learning methods may make systems stronger and easier to interpret. • Understanding implicit emotion and multimodality: Develop studies and models that focus on implicit emotional signals, not only on explicit emotion labels. Additionally, evaluate multimodal systems that combine different sources of information, such as speech, text, facial expressions, and physiological signals, and systematically remove one source at a time to clearly identify the contribution of each modality. • Better evaluation and more transparency: Develop testing standards that consider: — Uncertainty in emotion labels. — Unbalanced datasets. — Changes between training and real‑world conditions. — Pair performance scores with tools that show what parts of the sound the system paid attention to, and whether those parts match known acoustic patterns. • Responsible and fair deployment: For real ‑world applications (HCI, HRI, IoT), make sure systems handle privacy, consent, and fairness properly. This means documenting how data were collected, who is represented in the dataset, and how the system was checked for bias, not just for technical accuracy.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 35 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 10 Conclusion This review has brought together different research domains to show that the human voice carries meaningful traces of emotional and cognitive activity. Rather than treating speech as a purely linguistic signal, the evidence reviewed here highlights how changes in respiration, vocal‑fold behaviour, and articulation leave measurable acoustic marks. These patterns —shifts in pitch, loudness, spectral balance, and timing — are not random; they reflect underlying psychophysiological states in ways that both psychologists and engineers can make use of. Throughout the review, it has been emphasized that effective Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) depends as much on understanding how the voice works as on choosing the right computational tools. Clean preprocessing, thoughtful feature design or representation learning, and careful modelling choices are all important, but they make the most sense when grounded in vocal physiology and established acoustic correlations of emotion. Classical machine‑learning models are still relevant, especially when transparency or limited data are concerned, whereas deep and self ‑supervised approaches have opened the door to stronger generalization. Even so, the field has not identified a single optimal modelling “answer”, as it is unlikely that one model will satisfy all research needs. For applications in Human Computer Interaction (HCI), Human Robot Interaction (HRI), Internet of Things (IoT), and related domains, including emerging frameworks such as Neurocash ®, SER can serve as an additional layer of information about users’ implicit reactions. Combining vocal cues via SER with NLP or with other biometric modalities seems promising, particularly when the goal is to capture subtle affective or cognitive shifts rather than explicit emotional displays. The success of these approaches, however, will likely depend on more diverse and naturalistic datasets, as well as clearer evaluation practices that consider label uncertainty and the mismatch between controlled laboratory

data and real‑world settings. This becomes especially critical as perception studies for cash design have become increasingly important in recent years, demanding that the data obtained are sufficiently relevant to support reliable conclusions. In this context, modifying certain procedures—such as replacing on-screen response formats with the recording of participants’ vocal responses to questions presented on a screen—allows the direct application of SER to extract emotional information from speech, yielding richer data for cash design within the Neurocash® methodology. Finally, advances in SER must be accompanied by responsible treatment of privacy, consent, and fairness. Voice is a personal biometric, and emotion inference can raise concerns beyond those encountered in traditional speech processing. Clear documentation, careful dataset construction, and transparent model reporting will be essential if voice ‑based affective technologies are to be used in a way that is both scientifically grounded and socially acceptable.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 13
INFORME DE ESTABILIDAD FINANCIERA. OTOÑO 2024   PRINCIPALES VULNERABILIDADES Y RIESGOS PARA LA ESTABILIDAD FINANCIERA
Desde la publicación del pasado Informe de Estabilidad Financiera (IEF), se ha observado una 
evolución desigual de las vulnerabilidades y de los riesgos identificados (véase esquema 1).
De forma destacada, los riesgos vinculados a una inflación elevada se han reducido 
significativamente y de manera generalizada por geografías. También ha disminuido el 
riesgo de un menor crecimiento a corto plazo en España. En este contexto macroeconómico 
más favorable, la escalada de las tensiones geopolíticas continúa siendo el principal riesgo 
para la estabilidad financiera, que se ve incrementado por la intensificación de los conflictos 
en el este de Europa y en Oriente Próximo. Además, las valoraciones elevadas de algunos 
activos financieros con riesgo y otros factores, como la concentración del valor de los 
mercados de renta variable en un número reducido de empresas tecnológicas, aumentan 
los riesgos de correcciones abruptas en los mercados financieros. En cualquier caso, cabe 
señalar que los distintos riesgos identificados interaccionan entre sí y que la materialización 
de cualquiera de ellos puede agravar los otros.
PRINCIPALES VULNERABILIDADES Y RIESGOS PARA LA ESTABILIDAD FINANCIERA
Principales riesgos y vulnerabilidades para la estabilidad ﬁnanciera (a) (b) (c)
Esquema 1
RIESGOS 
FUENTE: Banco de España.
a En este Informe se deﬁnen en las vulnerabilidades  como aquellas condiciones económicas y ﬁnancieras que incrementan el impacto o la 
probabilidad de materialización de  los riesgos para la estabilidad ﬁnanciera.  Estos, a su vez, se identiﬁcan con variaciones adversas —y con 
una probabilidad de ocurrencia incierta— de las condiciones económicas y ﬁnancieras, o del entorno físico o geopolítico, que diﬁcultan o impiden 
la función de intermediación ﬁnanciera, con consecuencias negativas para la actividad económica real.
b Los riesgos y las vulnerabilidades que aparecen en este esquema se gradúan utilizando la siguiente escala: un bloque indica un nivel bajo (color 
amarillo), dos bloques un nivel medio (color naranja) y tres bloques un nivel alto (color rojo). Las ﬂechas señalan la evolución de los niveles de 
riesgos y vulnerabilidades desde el anterior IEF publicado.
c En el número anterior del IEF el riesgo R3 aparecía referido al incremento de la aversión al riesgo de los agentes, siendo su elemento principal una 
posible corrección abrupta en los mercados ﬁnancieros. Debido a la mayor importancia relativa de este elemento, se ha optado en este número por 
identiﬁcar al conjunto de este riesgo con el mismo.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 14 INFORME DE ESTABILIDAD FINANCIERA. OTOÑO 2024        PRINCIPALES VULNERABILIDADES Y RIESGOS PARA LA ESTABILIDAD FINANCIERA   
En cuanto al análisis de vulnerabilidades, el endeudamiento público ha seguido reduciéndose, 
aunque continúa siendo muy superior al promedio europeo. En este contexto, avanzar en el 
calendario de implementación de las nuevas reglas fiscales europeas, disminuir el nivel de 
déficit estructural y asegurar el proceso de consolidación de las cuentas públicas en España 
requieren una adecuada ejecución del Plan Fiscal y Estructural de Medio Plazo (PFEMP) 
recientemente anunciado. Por su parte, los hogares y las empresas no financieras mantienen 
la buena evolución de sus rentas y continúan el proceso de reducción de sus ratios de 
endeudamiento para disminuir su grado de vulnerabilidad financiera.
La situación financiera del sector bancario español se mantiene favorable, con una rentabilidad 
elevada, apoyada en la buena evolución del margen de interés y, en menor medida, de las 
comisiones netas. No obstante, esto no se ha traducido en un refuerzo significativo de sus 
ratios de solvencia, y la ratio de CET1 ha permanecido comparativamente reducida en relación 
con otros sistemas bancarios europeos. A escala global, se mantiene la preocupación por el 
elevado apalancamiento y la acumulación de riesgos de liquidez en algunos intermediarios 
financieros no bancarios (IFNB).
A continuación se exponen con mayor detalle los principales riesgos 1 para la estabilidad del 
sistema financiero español:
R1. Riesgos geopolíticos
La escalada regional del conflicto de Oriente Próximo y la intensificación de las acciones 
ofensivas en la guerra entre Rusia y Ucrania elevan los riesgos geopolíticos, lo que incrementa 
la probabilidad de una escalada y una extensión aún mayores de estos conflictos.
La valoración de otras fuentes de riesgos geopolíticos se mantiene relativamente estable 
desde primavera, pero en un nivel también elevado que hace necesario continuar con su 
monitorización. En concreto, son de especial relevancia las tensiones comerciales de China 
con Estados Unidos, así como con la Unión Europea, que afectan a distintos bienes, pero de 
forma particular a ciertos productos tecnológicos (véase gráfico 1). Estos son necesarios para 
sostener y avanzar la digitalización de las actividades económicas y también para la transición 
hacia una economía más sostenible, ambos desarrollos clave para el crecimiento económico 
a largo plazo.
De forma relacionada, las elecciones presidenciales de Estados Unidos implican incertidumbre 
sobre la orientación de las políticas de este país cuyos efectos tienen un alcance global. 
Previsiblemente, el desenlace de estas elecciones será el evento geopolítico más relevante de 
los próximos meses. En el ámbito europeo, los resultados de las elecciones de algunos

Se sigue manteniendo la posibilidad de intensificación a escala global de ciberataques con

Por el momento, el efecto de las tensiones geopolíticas sobre la actividad económica

Sin embargo, si se materializara un escenario de escalada global de tensiones geopolíticas, 
sería posible experimentar perturbaciones negativas de oferta de mayor intensidad y un 
deterioro generalizado de la confianza de los inversores, con consecuencias muy adversas 
sobre la actividad económica y financiera mundial y también sobre la inflación. Esta podría 
verse afectada en particular a través de disrupciones en las cadenas internacionales de

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 16 INFORME DE ESTABILIDAD FINANCIERA. OTOÑO 2024        PRINCIPALES VULNERABILIDADES Y RIESGOS PARA LA ESTABILIDAD FINANCIERA   
El mantenimiento de tensiones geopolíticas durante períodos extensos condiciona además 
distintas políticas públicas (por ejemplo, aumento del proteccionismo comercial, incremento 
del gasto militar y del tamaño de los ejércitos) y eleva la probabilidad de que se consolide una 
dinámica de bloques. Esta revertiría las ganancias de eficiencia de la globalización —por 
ejemplo, a través de un aumento generalizado de los aranceles— y podría disminuir la 
capacidad de absorción de perturbaciones futuras.
La valoración del resto de los riesgos en este resumen está condicionada por un nivel global 
estable de las tensiones geopolíticas; otras perturbaciones que pueden afectar a la estabilidad 
del sistema financiero español se evalúan de manera separada. El recuadro 1.1 analiza de 
forma más amplia los canales de riesgos comerciales para la UE y para España vinculados a 
las tensiones geopolíticas.
R2. Riesgo de inflación más elevada y persistente
En los últimos meses, el proceso de corrección de la inflación ha continuado a escala global, 
aunque se ha visto limitado por la persistencia de las presiones inflacionistas en los servicios 
(véase gráfico 3). A pesar de este factor de resistencia, las expectativas de inflación a corto 
plazo han mostrado una corrección a la baja desde abril, sobre todo en Estados Unidos, y son 
coherentes con la prolongación futura del proceso desinflacionario.

INFORME DE ESTABILIDAD FINANCIERA. OTOÑO 2024   PRINCIPALES VULNERABILIDADES Y RIESGOS PARA LA ESTABILIDAD FINANCIERA
En el área del euro, la inflación ha mantenido una tendencia descendente en los últimos 
meses y, de hecho, de forma transitoria se ha situado por debajo del objetivo de política 
monetaria, al reducirse hasta el 1,7 % interanual en septiembre de 2024. Este comportamiento 
se debe no solo a la disminución de la inflación de la energía y de los alimentos, sino también 
a la reducción de la inflación subyacente, lo que refleja, en buena medida, que el proceso de 
endurecimiento de la política monetaria ha conseguido mantener ancladas las expectativas 
de inflación de los agentes. En España, la inflación se situó también en el 1,7 % en septiembre2, 
y su evolución, en líneas generales, mostró un perfil y unos determinantes similares a los del 
conjunto del área del euro. 
En cualquier caso, las proyecciones del Banco Central Europeo (BCE) siguen apuntando a 
una evolución de la inflación hacia el objetivo del 2 % a medio plazo, tanto en el conjunto del 
área del euro como en España. En este entorno, el Consejo de Gobierno del BCE ha reducido 
en tres ocasiones, en junio, septiembre y octubre, en 25 puntos básicos (pb) los tipos de 
interés oficiales. 
El Consejo de Gobierno del BCE ha continuado indicando que las posibles reducciones 
adicionales futuras de los tipos de interés de política monetaria estarán condicionadas por los 
datos que se vayan recibiendo. Desde la publicación del último IEF, las expectativas de 
mercado se han orientado hacia mayores reducciones de estos tipos y, de forma consistente, 
hacia menores tipos de interés a corto y largo plazo en el área del euro (véase gráfico 4). 
Los mercados laborales del área del euro mantienen un comportamiento dinámico, aunque 
se observan señales de mayor holgura y cierta moderación del crecimiento de los salarios, si 
bien este sería suficiente para permitir a los trabajadores recuperar progresivamente la renta 
real perdida en años anteriores. Esta moderación podría ser un factor clave para contener las 
presiones inflacionistas en el sector servicios, aunque, por el momento, estas se mantienen 
como la principal preocupación en este ámbito.
Es también todavía relevante la posibilidad de una mayor persistencia de la inflación en 
Estados Unidos con respecto a las expectativas, que podría ajustar al alza la senda de tipos 
de interés de su política monetaria, endureciendo las condiciones financieras globales. 
En sentido contrario, una materialización de riesgos a la baja sobre el crecimiento, en 
un contexto en el que se observan algunos síntomas de debilidad en la demanda global, o 
un mayor impacto potencial de las políticas monetarias vigentes podrían conducir a una 
inflación más baja de lo proyectado. En particular, una mayor moderación del crecimiento en 
China puede contribuir, a través de distintos canales financieros y comerciales, a una menor 
inflación en otras economías, fundamentalmente por sus efectos sobre la demanda global 
de materias primas.

R3. Riesgo de una corrección abrupta de las valoraciones en los mercados financieros
Las métricas de incertidumbre en los mercados financieros se mantienen en niveles históricamente 
reducidos (véase gráfico 5) a pesar del entorno de elevadas tensiones geopolíticas y la persistencia 
de algunos riesgos sobre la evolución de la inflación y el crecimiento.
Asimismo, las primas de riesgo de distintos activos financieros se sitúan en niveles históricamente 
bajos. De forma destacada, esto se observa en los mercados de renta variable de Estados 
Unidos, pero también en otras categorías de activos, como la renta fija corporativa de alto 
rendimiento, de origen tanto europeo como estadounidense (véase gráfico 6).
La persistencia de valoraciones elevadas de los activos financieros con riesgo en la actual 
coyuntura de incertidumbre puede hacer frágiles las percepciones de los inversores. Incluso 
en ausencia de materialización de grandes perturbaciones asociadas a los riesgos 
geopolíticos, variaciones limitadas de las condiciones macrofinancieras pueden volver más 
pesimistas a los inversores y propiciar correcciones abruptas de los precios en los mercados 
financieros. El episodio de turbulencias experimentado al inicio de agosto (caída brusca del 
valor del mercado de renta variable de Japón y, en menor medida, de otras geografías) ilustra 
esta fragilidad.

A la hora de valorar los riesgos en los mercados financieros, es necesario considerar también 
la elevada concentración del valor del mercado de renta variable en el sector tecnológico, en 
particular en un número reducido de empresas de Estados Unidos (véase recuadro 1.2). De 
esta manera, perturbaciones en las expectativas sobre el valor de nuevas tecnologías (por 
ejemplo, la inteligencia artificial) o sobre la capacidad de distintas empresas de retener las 
ganancias de eficiencia generadas por estas pueden propiciar oscilaciones significativas en 
la capitalización de los índices bursátiles.
Aunque la concentración tecnológica y otros factores de riesgo sobre los mercados financieros 
aparecen ligados específicamente a Estados Unidos, la posición central de su sistema 
financiero en los mercados mundiales y el elevado grado de interconexiones entre ellos hacen 
que estos factores tengan relevancia global. 
En un escenario de correcciones de valoración, como ya se ha señalado en ediciones 
anteriores del IEF, existe un riesgo específico de ampliación de estas por el comportamiento 
procíclico de distintos IFNB. En algunos segmentos de este sector (por ejemplo, hedge funds, 
family offices ) se continúa detectando un apalancamiento elevado y señales de acumulación 
de riesgos de liquidez, lo que hace que su comportamiento sea más sensible a distintas 
perturbaciones.
Este escenario de materialización de riesgos en los mercados financieros también afectaría 
negativamente a las entidades bancarias, al endurecer sus condiciones de financiación 
mayorista. 
R4. Riesgo a la baja sobre el crecimiento económico
El tono de la actividad económica mundial sigue siendo, en términos generales, positivo y 
algo más dinámico de lo anticipado en el anterior IEF (véase gráfico 7), aunque también 
persisten algunos síntomas de debilidad. En el área del euro, la actividad económica mantuvo 
un tono débil en la primera mitad de 2024 y se espera una recuperación lenta y gradual, algo 
inferior a la prevista la primavera pasada, con un crecimiento que se mantendría, en cualquier 
caso, en tasas reducidas a medio plazo. 
Los indicadores de corto plazo apuntan a un menor vigor en el tercer trimestre en distintas 
geografías, y los datos recientes sugieren una desaceleración global de la actividad manufacturera 
y resistencia de los servicios. 
La economía española mantuvo un elevado grado de dinamismo en el primer semestre del 
año, y su crecimiento estuvo claramente por encima del observado en el conjunto del área 
del euro. Además, se revisaron al alza las estimaciones de los años inmediatamente 
posteriores a la pandemia, anticipando significativamente la recuperación de los niveles de 
PIB previos a esta. El crecimiento del PIB español en los últimos trimestres se ha sustentado 
en la demanda exterior neta, tanto por el vigor mostrado por las exportaciones (especialmente

Por su parte, el cumplimiento de las nuevas reglas fiscales europeas puede suponer cierto 
freno al crecimiento en los próximos años, si bien constituirá un resorte para reforzar la 
sostenibilidad de las cuentas públicas. Existen ciertos elementos mitigadores de estos riesgos 
sobre la actividad. Por una parte, una política monetaria menos restrictiva en las principales 
economías mundiales proporcionaría mayor soporte al crecimiento a corto plazo. Por otra 
parte, a escala nacional, la elevada tasa de ahorro de los hogares y el impacto de los proyectos 
asociados al programa Next Generation EU (NGEU) pueden constituir palancas de apoyo 
para el consumo y la inversión, respectivamente.
Finalmente, también en el ámbito nacional, cabe destacar que la actual composición del 
crecimiento puede persistir como una vulnerabilidad de la economía española incluso si se 
consolida la actual senda expansiva y se disipan los riesgos a corto plazo sobre la actividad 
(véase gráfico 8). Por el lado del gasto, el crecimiento del PIB ha estado sostenido en una 
proporción relevante por la demanda externa de servicios, especialmente los turísticos, y por 
el consumo público, frente a una menor contribución del consumo privado y, en particular, de 
la inversión empresarial. Por el lado de las ramas de actividad, se observa una contribución 
elevada al crecimiento de servicios de baja productividad (por ejemplo, la hostelería). 
En este contexto, las principales vulnerabilidades 3 de la economía y del sistema financiero 
español incluyen:
V1. Nivel elevado de endeudamiento público
El déficit de las Administraciones Públicas, en términos acumulados de 12 meses, se habría 
situado en el 3,3 % en junio, lo que supone una reducción de 0,2 puntos porcentuales (pp) 
respecto al cierre de 2023. La ratio de deuda pública sobre PIB se redujo 3,5 pp en términos 
interanuales, fundamentalmente por el aumento del PIB nominal, y se situó en el 105,3 % en 
el segundo trimestre de 2024. Este nivel de endeudamiento público es unos 20 pp inferior al 
máximo alcanzado tras el inicio de la pandemia, en marzo de 2021, aunque supera en cerca 
de 18 pp al del agregado del área del euro (véase gráfico 9).
El coste medio de las nuevas emisiones de deuda ascendió al 3,3 % en los ocho primeros 
meses de 2024, 0,2 pp por debajo de su nivel medio de 2023. El coste medio de las emisiones 
más recientes, en septiembre, fue del 2,9 %, lo que refleja las perspectivas de una menor 
restricción monetaria. No obstante, se prevé que continúe el aumento progresivo del coste 
medio del saldo vivo, dado que la vida media de la deuda pública española está próxima a 
los ocho años y que las emisiones puestas en circulación entre 2016 y 2021 se emitían

mercados financieros.
En ausencia de la aplicación de las nuevas reglas fiscales europeas, la senda de la deuda 
pública y de los pagos por intereses sería moderadamente creciente en los próximos años. 
Esto es resultado del elevado componente estructural del déficit público español y de ciertos 
factores que presionarán al alza el gasto público, como el envejecimiento de la población, las 
necesidades de inversión asociadas al cambio climático, la digitalización y el gasto en defensa. 
No debe olvidarse que el elevado nivel de deuda pública aumenta la sensibilidad del gasto a los 
cambios en las condiciones de financiación en los mercados. Si además se tiene en cuenta la 
necesidad de generar espacio fiscal para mitigar el impacto de posibles perturbaciones adversas, 
parece estrictamente necesario que el plan de consolidación fiscal recientemente anunciado en 
España, junto con determinadas reformas estructurales, se ejecuten con diligencia y rigor para 
corregir esta vulnerabilidad y minimizar su impacto en la actividad. Esto es especialmente 
relevante en tanto que el plan propone un perfil temporal con un crecimiento del gasto que 
disminuye en el tiempo, lo que facilita su cumplimiento en los primeros años, en los que se asume 
una posición cíclica más favorable, y se torna más restrictivo hacia el final del periodo de ajuste4.

INFORME DE ESTABILIDAD FINANCIERA. OTOÑO 2024   PRINCIPALES VULNERABILIDADES Y RIESGOS PARA LA ESTABILIDAD FINANCIERA
V2. Debilidad financiera de empresas no financieras y hogares
Las empresas no financieras españolas han mantenido en la primera mitad de 2024 una 
buena evolución de sus resultados, al tiempo que continúa el proceso de reducción de su 
ratio de endeudamiento en términos del PIB. Todo ello ha redundado en una reducción de sus 
vulnerabilidades financieras.
Los excedentes empresariales mostraron un comportamiento favorable en la primera mitad 
de 2024, aunque de forma heterogénea por sectores. El resultado económico bruto (REB)5 del 
sector empresarial no financiero, de acuerdo con la información de la Agencia Tributaria, 
aumentó, en términos nominales, en el primer trimestre de 2024 un 6,5 % interanual y un 
9,2 % en el segundo trimestre.
Por su parte, los datos de la Encuesta del Banco de España sobre la actividad empresarial 
(EBAE) del tercer trimestre muestran un descenso de las presiones inflacionistas sobre los 
precios de venta y los costes de inputs intermedios y laborales. Además, se identifican 
condiciones más favorables en términos de acceso y coste de la financiación. Persisten, sin 
embargo, las preocupaciones por la incertidumbre sobre las políticas económicas, la 
disponibilidad de mano de obra y posibles repuntes de los costes energéticos.
En este contexto, la deuda consolidada de las empresas no financieras españolas presentó 
un incremento interanual del 1,3 % hasta junio de 2024. Sin embargo, el endeudamiento de 
este sector se situó en el 65 % del PIB en el segundo trimestre del año (véase gráfico 10), 
3,6 pp menos que 12 meses antes, el valor más bajo registrado de la serie desde septiembre 
de 2002. Adicionalmente, esta ratio era 1,8 pp inferior a la media de este sector en el conjunto 
del área del euro, que alcanzaba el 66,8 % en ese mismo período.
Por su parte, el sector de los hogares también redujo sus vulnerabilidades financieras, 
apoyado en la resiliencia del empleo, el crecimiento de la renta bruta disponible (RBD) y la 
reducción de su deuda en relación con el PIB 6.
En concreto, la tasa de paro de la Encuesta de Población Activa (EPA) se situaba en junio de 
2024 en el 11,3 %, 0,4 pp menos que 12 meses antes, cifra no observada desde el tercer 
trimestre de 2008. En este contexto, la RBD real media por hogar7 ha mostrado un crecimiento 
interanual medio del 3,8 % (frente al 4,4 % del semestre precedente) y se sitúa un 2,8 % por 
encima del nivel anterior a la pandemia 8. El volumen de deuda de las familias aumentó en el 
segundo trimestre del año, por primera vez desde el verano de 2022, al tiempo que su riqueza

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 24 INFORME DE ESTABILIDAD FINANCIERA. OTOÑO 2024        PRINCIPALES VULNERABILIDADES Y RIESGOS PARA LA ESTABILIDAD FINANCIERA   
bruta continuó incrementándose. El mayor avance de las rentas en comparación con el 
incremento de los niveles de deuda permitió que la ratio de endeudamiento de las familias se 
redujera hasta el 44,9 % del PIB en el segundo trimestre de 2024, nivel no observado desde 
el año 2000 y 7,5 pp inferior al promedio del área del euro. 
A pesar de estos desarrollos positivos en términos de renta y de endeudamiento, los costes 
medios de la deuda y la carga financiera de hogares y empresas no financieras se mantienen 
en valores comparativamente elevados en relación con el per íodo de tipos de interés bajos 
posterior a la crisis financiera global. El ajuste progresivo de la política monetaria y los plazos 
de revisión en los contratos a tipo variable hacen esperar que el descenso de la carga 
financiera de estos sectores sea gradual, manteniendo así los agentes endeudados cierto 
grado de vulnerabilidad a corto plazo.
En concreto, la ratio de carga financiera (gastos por intereses sobre excedente bruto de 
explotación) de las empresas no financieras aumentó en el segundo trimestre de 2024 hasta 
el 17,7 %, 5,3 pp por encima de la cifra registrada 12 meses antes, el nivel más elevado de esta 
métrica desde 2012 (véase el panel derecho del gráfico 10). En la Central de Balances 
Trimestral (CBT), la proporción de empresas vulnerables no experimentó variaciones 
interanuales significativas hasta junio de 2024, con un comportamiento mixto de distintos 
indicadores de fragilidad financiera (por ejemplo, resultados negativos, carga financiera 
elevada). En todo caso, estos indicadores se sitúan por debajo del promedio observado en el 
período 2014-2023.
En el caso de los hogares, la ratio agregada de carga financiera (gastos financieros sobre 
RBD) se situaba en un 2,9 % en junio de 2024, con un incremento interanual de 0,5 pp (véase, 
de nuevo, el panel derecho del gráfico 10). Este nivel de carga financiera representa el valor 
más elevado de la serie desde 2014.
La buena evolución de la renta continúa conteniendo el incremento de la proporción de 
hogares con una carga financiera bruta elevada (superior al 40 % de la renta del hogar). No 
obstante, en este per íodo la inflación, en particular sobre el coste de consumos esenciales 
como los alimentos y la energía, ha presionado adicionalmente la capacidad de pago de sus 
compromisos financieros.
V3. Debilidades en la capacidad de intermediación del sector financiero
La rentabilidad del sector bancario español siguió aumentando en el primer semestre de 2024 
y alcanzó unas ratios ROA (rentabilidad sobre el total activo, por sus siglas en inglés) y ROE 
(rentabilidad sobre patrimonio neto, por sus siglas en inglés) del 0,91 % y el 13,9 %, 
respectivamente, 16 pb y 2,2 pp superiores a las registradas en junio de 2023. 
El proceso de incremento de los tipos de política monetaria ha propiciado un aumento 
generalizado de la rentabilidad de los bancos europeos, en el que las entidades españolas se

de rentabilidad de los bancos españoles no se ha trasladado a una mejora de su posición

requerimientos adicionales de capital, como la activación del colchón de capital anticíclico 
(CCA) sobre exposiciones en España, descrita más abajo.
Los distintos componentes del beneficio bancario mantienen el mismo patrón cualitativo de 
evolución observado en 2023, con un crecimiento marcado del margen de interés como 
principal impulsor de la rentabilidad y una contribución más moderada de las comisiones 
netas y otros componentes del margen bruto, que, en conjunto, más que compensan la 
evolución negativa de otras partidas, como las dotaciones por deterioro. Estas últimas 
continúan presentando un crecimiento contenido a pesar del rápido e intenso ascenso de los 
tipos de interés de referencia desde 2022. Por su parte, los gastos de explotación continuaron 
evolucionando al alza en un entorno inflacionario, y el gravamen a la actividad crediticia en 
España siguió detrayendo una parte limitada de la rentabilidad (en su ausencia, el ROA de 
junio de 2024 hubiera sido 4 pb superior y hubiera alcanzado el 0,95 %, y el ROE hubiera sido 
0,6 pp mayor, hasta el 14,5 %). En términos de los activos ponderados por riesgo (APR) a junio 
de 2024 el gravamen representó un 0,11 %.
De cara al futuro, en el entorno de los escenarios de previsión, el impacto de la bajada de tipos de 
interés sobre la rentabilidad bancaria sería acotado y gradual, al compensarse, al menos en 
parte, los potenciales efectos negativos sobre márgenes unitarios con una evolución más 
favorable del volumen de actividad y de las dotaciones por deterioros y contar las entidades 
con distintos instrumentos de gestión del riesgo de interés. Los resultados de las pruebas de 
resistencia del Banco de España9 muestran, de hecho, que el sector bancario español retendría 
capacidad de generación orgánica de capital bajo este tipo de escenarios (véase gráfico 12).
En contraste, la materialización de los riesgos macrofinancieros identificados mermaría 
significativamente la rentabilidad del sector y, bajo el escenario más adverso (con 
materialización intensa de múltiples riesgos) (véase recuadro 2.1), los resultados de las 
pruebas de resistencia indican que llegaría a producirse cierto nivel de consumo de capital 
(véase, de nuevo, el gráfico 12). Estos resultados denotan una notable capacidad de resistencia 
a escala agregada del sector bancario español. Sin embargo, la reducción de su solvencia en 
este escenario más adverso limitaría su capacidad de intermediación y haría esperable un cierto 
grado de desapalancamiento, también presente, aunque con menor intensidad, en escenarios 
de materialización más parcial de riesgos sistémicos.

cantidad de riesgos y con menor intensidad, la rentabilidad del sector bancario español se
